PRESS REPORT AS TO APPEAL OF LORD WOOLTON TO UNITED STATES-VOLUNTARY CREAMLESS DAYS *
On the orders of the day:

I wish to ask a question of the Minister of Agriculture. 
In view of the appeal made by Lord Woolton, head of the British food control, to the housewives of the United States to inaugurate a "creamless day" in order that it may be made possible to use the milk thereby saved for the manufacture of milk powder which is urgently needed in Great Britain, and also in view of the item in the New York Daily Neivs with the heading "No Creamless Days in Canada", would the minister advise the house and the country if it is the government's intention to do anything with regard to this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The hon. member was kind
enough to give me an intimation of the fact that he intended to ask this question, and I have prepared the following answer:
We have had no information with regard to Lord Woolton's appeal to the American people other than what has appeared in the press.
It has been intimated' to us from Britain that they would like us to turn all the milk possible into cheese and supply it to Britain.
The price of 14-4 cents on boat at Montreal offered by Britain is all that they can be expected to pay, as it is on a parity with what they are paying New Zealand. The Canadian government is, therefore, paying 1-6 cents above that price in addition to one cent premium on 93 score cheese and two cents on 94 score cheese. The Ontario and Quebec governments are adding as much as two cents a pound. Under these provisions the Canadian people are paying from 4-6 to 5-6 cents a pound in addition to the 14-4 cents which Britain is paying on practically all the cheese going to Great Britain, or about one-quarter of the return to the producer. This is being done to assure that this year and next the highest possible production of cheese will be made available to the British people.
To make doubly sure that the additional production thus secured will go to Britain the daily board commandeered all cheese coming on the market from May 26 forward until further notice in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec where 93 per cent of all the cheese is made.
It will thus be seen that although we have not adopted the plan suggested in the United States we have met the appeal of Britain in the manner suggested. This fact has had the widest publicity and I am sure the method adopted is accepted by the British government as the best possible way of providing the greatest possible quantity of Canadian dairy products to Britain.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when you put the question I was on my feet to make just the sort of statement which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) has quite properly asked for.
It is quite true, as the leader of the opposition has remarked, that the provisions of this measure are somewhat unusual. I shall deal with that presently. It might be of interest to the house, however, if I gave a brief history of the development of the Banff national park and the condition's leading up to the proposals embodied in this bill.
The mineral springs that led to the setting aside of the Banff area were first discovered in 18S3. In 1885 the government of the day passed an order in council setting aside ten square miles around these mineral springs. In 1887 the Rocky Mountains Park Act was passed, and at the same time the area in what is now the Banff park was increased to 260 square miles. In 1902 the act was amended increasing the area to 4,400 square miles. By order in council, in July 1892, under the Dominion Lands Act-another act altogether-the lake Louise area of 51 square miles was set aside as a forest park. The Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act in 1911 repealed the Rocky Mountains Park Act. If hon. gentlemen will give their attention to this they will get the sequence of the story right through. The act passed in 1911 provided that "the governor in council may from time to time, by proclamation, designate such reserves or areas within forest reserves, as he sees fit, to be known as dominion parks.'' At the same time the park area was reduced to 1,800 square miles. In 1917 by order in council the area

was again increased to 2,751 square miles, and in 1929 a further 103 square miles were added to it.
In 1930 the natural resources of the prairie provinces were transferred to those provinces. Prior to that they had been held in the right of the crown in the federal government and administered by the federal government. In the same year the National Parks Act was passed by parliament, giving more direct control over park areas, and the name Rocky Mountains park, which up to that date had described what is now the Banff park, was changed to the Banff National Park. I might say in passing that the effect of the National Parks Act was to vest more authority in parliament than had theretofore been the case, in this particular, that no park could be created anywhere in Canada without an act of parliament, nor could the boundaries of a park be either increased or reduced without an act amending the act creating the park.
I wish now to deal briefly with the hydro power development in this particular area. About 1909 or a little earlier the Calgary Power Company was incorporated, and in 1909 it developed on the Bow river, at what was known as the Horseshoe falls, a hydro plant having a capacity of 20,000 horse-power.

Since 1912 the Calgary Power company have on several occasions made application to secure more water from within the park area. Applications for storage and power privileges have been steadily refused by all governments down to the present time. It will be recalled by some hon. members, at any rate those from western Canada who are familiar with the matter, that between 1922 and 1930 there was considerable agitation over an application that the company had made to secure the right to put certain works on what were known as the Spray lakes, which were within the park area. The view was generally held in western Canada, and indeed in eastern Canada as well, that since the national parks were created as national playgrounds no industrial development should be permitted within the parks which would detract from their beauty and the purpose for which they were created. At the same time it was recognized that the power company required additional water. As a result of the discussions that took place at the time the resources were
transferred to Alberta, the Spray lakes area was taken out of the park altogether. Then it became a matter for the Alberta government to deal with the power company in the disposition of the water from the Spray lakes. Nothing further was done, though I believe the company made application for and secured from the Alberta government the right to develop, but of that I am not sure at the moment. At any rate nothing further was done so far as the Spray lakes development was concerned. That is the history of the power development down to last autumn.
I come now to another phase of the story. Last November the Department of Munitions and Supply reached the conclusion, after a close study of the facts, that it was very necessary to set up an ammonium nitrate plant at Calgary. I am not familiar with the requirements of an ammonium nitrate plant, but natural gas, of which there is a large quantity in that particular area in Alberta, is a necessary material entering into the production of the nitrates that the plant is intended to produce.
There arose then the question of power. The Calgary Power company were approached and they stated that they were not in a position to guarantee the amount of power that would be required by the new plant. The amount was estimated by the engineers of the Department of Munitions and Supply, or of the government-created company, Allied War Supplies Corporation, at 23,000 horsepower. What was needed was a dependable supply of power to the amount of 23,000 horse-power. Consequently the Department of Mines and Resources was approached by the Department of Munitions and Supply, or rather by the company, first to inquire if we would agree to the erection of storage facilities at lake Minnewanka that would provide not only the necessary supply of water during the winter months but also for a new power plant to be built near Anthracite close to the lake which would produce the power required for the chemical plant.

In regard to steam turbine equipment, such equipment is not made in Canada. It would have to be secured either from Great Britain or from the United States. Inquiry was made by the officials of the Department of Mines and Resources as to the length of time which might be required to procure this equipment. It could have been procured from Great Britain in about twelve months, if everything had worked out favourably, but there was the possibility that the plants manufacturing steam turbine equipment might be bombed, with consequent delay in the delivery of the equipment, together with the even greater risk of the equipment being lost through enemy action while in transit from Britain to Canada. So far as United States sources of supply were concerned, it was ascertained that no guarantee could be obtained in that country that the equipment would be delivered within two years. Those are the points I wished to emphasize. On November 15 my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply wrote me in reply to my letter in which

I had set out the alternatives of steam turbine development and the Spray lakes development. The letter was as follows:
I have your letter of the 13th instant. The ammonia plant of the Alberta Nitrogen Company is scheduled to go into operation by the first of September next, and it is of the utmost importance to our war effort that the plant be assured of an adequate power supply from that date on. To be assured of power, a development must be made, and none of the possible alternatives to the lake Minnewanka development -would	afford this	assurance.	TheSpray Lakes site	is difficult of	access	and
involves the construction of a high dam and a two mile tunnel. It could not be built in less than two years. It is a much larger project than is required, and the company is not in a position to undertake it.
As regards a steam power station, the plants manufacturing steam turbines are congested with orders, and	deliveries	are	long	anduncertain. Even if priorities adequate for the purpose could be	obtained,	they	would	be
subject to the control of other governments, and, therefore, hazardous. Turbines from Britain would be subject to conditions in Britain and shipping risks. I am informed that in Edmonton, where coal is exceedingly cheap, the cost of steam power is far in excess of the price which the power company is quoting to the Allied War Supplies Corporation under the contract, and that the price of coal in Calgary would be substantially more than in Edmonton, with the consequent increased cost of power. As a result, and after investigation, the Allied War Supplies Corporation decided that the economic and feasible thing to do was to contract with the company. Furthermore, the power company is unwilling, under all the circumstances, to invest in a steam plant, and, if steam were selected, the dominion government would be faced with the financing of the construction and would have an uneconomical plant left on its hands after the war.
The lake Minnewanka development is simple to construct. No coffer damming or unwatering is required, and the site is accessible by good roads. The machinery would all be manufactured in Canada, and the promises of deliveries are such that the plant could be completed in time even without priorities, and, in any event, would be subject to our right to order priorities.
I am informed by the company that even at this late date, by putting temporary cribbing on the existing dam and by deepening the power canal, sufficient additional water can be made available to meet the requirements of the ammonia plant in the first season of operations.
With respect to the suggestion of scenery, there seems to be a difference of opinion as to whether or not the scenery would be improved.
With respect to the small government hydro plant, compensation will, of course, have to be paid for this.
With respect to the methods of granting the licence, it can, of course, be granted under the War Measures Act, but because of the amount of money involved the company has stipulated for an act of parliament. I see no reason why the licence cannot be granted under the War Measures Act and the necessary legislation passed at this session, but if for any reason this is considered objectionable, I have no doubt

Alberta Natural Resources
the company would be prepared to accept the assurance of the government that the act would be passed. Whichever method is adopted, it is essential that work be started immediately, and work cannot be started until the assurance of a licence is given to the company.
Yours faithfully,
C. D. Howe.

So that the Alberta government placed itself squarely behind the proposal. I should say that the question was very carefully considered by the government as a whole, and it was only the urgent necessity of securing a dependable supply of power which would enable this chemical plant to get into operation at the earliest possible day, and ensure its continuance in operation, that led the government to the decision that the storage reservoir at lake Minnewanka should be proceeded with.

As the proposed project is, on the representations made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, clearly required for war purposes, I am of opinion that it would be competent to the governor in council, under and by virtue of the powers conferred by the War Measures Act, to grant your minister authority to permit the company to commence the construction of the works contemplated by its application upon the terms and conditions proposed.

e made to grant the company interim permission under authority given by this order in council and, as I said a moment ago, with the provision that it had to be approved by parliament. The licence has all the safeguards provided for under the regulations of the general Dominion Water Power Act. That act is of long standing, and the regulations under it are those which have governed power development throughout the country for a great many years.
In addition the licence contains special provisions designed to protect the natural beauty of the park. In. 'the main these may be summarized as follows: In carrying out the proposal, the level of the lake will be raised from 4,775 feet, the present maximum, to a maximum of 4,840, or a total of 65 feet. It is estimated that not more than 30 feet of water will be drawn off the reservoir during the winter months at any time, to ensure the full supply of water necessary for the operation of these plants. So that the minimum low level is raised about 35 feet from its present maximum.
In doing that a very considerable area is bound to be flooded. The provisions of the licence, I believe, are ample to ensure that the work done by the company in clearing around the present shores of the lake shall be carried on in such a way as to detract as little as possible from the natural beauty of the lake. Consequently the licence contains definite provisions for clearing and close cutting of timber, and the taking out of the stumps on the part of the shore which might
Alberta Natural Resources

be subject to flooding or wave action. This is all being done to the satisfaction of the minister of the department.
In addition the company agrees to the release of sufficient water at any time the park authorities may require it for any purpose. It is anticipated that this will be required only for possible fire fighting purposes. In addition the company agrees to the construction at its cost of new roads, trails, wharves and so on, to replace those flooded or damaged, including a new road across the dam, and following the water conduit down to Anthracite, where the power plant will be established. The proposal is that a new power plant will be built. The licence provides that it has to be to a design satisfactory to the park authorities or to the minister.
The canal which will be made to carry the water to the new power plant will be constructed in a manner satisfactory to the parks authorities and to the minister, and in accordance with the dominion water power regulations. The dam itself will be of earthen construction. It will be very substantial, since, as I said a moment ago, the purpose is to raise the maximum level of the lake by at least 65 feet. The company agrees to provide a proper road across the top of the dam and down to Anthracite, perhaps a mile and a half or so, where it will connect with the road from Calgary to Banff, and to maintain these works in a way which will detract as little as possible from the scenic value-and if possible, in time, when trees and shrubs are planted, increase the scenic value.
To ensure that these works are carried out in accordance with the provisions of the licence the department has retained the services of Doctor Thomas Hogg, chairman of the Ontario hydro commission, to act in a consulting capacity. We have also retained the services of a landscape architect who is to study the effect of the proposed works on the scenic value. The company agrees to pay the expenses and remuneration of both these consultants.

The period of the licence is to be for fifty years from the date of completion of the authorized

works, the rental for storage and power rights during the twenty years following the date of completion of the works to be the same as under the interim licence. I shall give further details with respect to that in a moment.
This is subject to revision after twenty years, and every ten years thereafter. That is, for twenty years the rental for storage and water paid by the company is fixed. After that it comes up for reconsideration at the end of twenty years, and every ten years thereafter, until fifty years have expired. The rental for lands occupied is to be fixed for a period of fifty years. All rights held and obligations assumed by the company under the agreement of March 1, 1912, are to cease from the date of completion of the works.

to reimburse them for any loss they may sustain. The company also agrees to build new wharves where such may be necessary.
I think, Mr. Speaker, I have covered in a general way the main provisions of the agreement. Let me summarize, as follows:
The changes in the level of the lake are to be brought about in such fashion as will detract in the least degree possible from the scenic value. The works are to be built and landscaped on the suggestions of the land*-scape architect which the department has employed and which the company pays for, subject to this, that if there is a difference of opinion between the landscape architect and the company's engineers as to what work should be done, it will be referred to the minister, and his decision is to be final.
The power plant is to be built of a design satisfactory to the park authorities, and the dam and other works are to be treated in a similar way.
The government in its administration of Banff park is protected in the matter of electrical energy, in that it is to be maintained in its present position so far as the supply of power and electrical energy to the park is concerned.
I recognize, and I sympathize with, the very widely held view that our national parks should be kept as free as possible from industrialization of any kind; that they should be maintained as great natural beauty spots. This was the purpose of the parks act, and during the last fifteen or twenty years that purpose has been consistently carried out. As minister in charge of the administration of the parks-and in what I am about to say I speak for the government-I can say that these works would not have been agreed to had it not been that we were convinced of the urgency of a war need. The production of ammonium nitrates is vital to the manufacture of munitions of war. As I stated earlier, the plant was located at Calgary because the necessary quantities of natural gas were available.
We are in a desperate war. We do not know how many dreary, heavy months lie ahead. We do know this, that if we are to succeed, the implements and the equipment of war, the guns, the tanks, the aeroplanes and the munitions, must be supplied. The government felt that under the circumstances this plant should be brought into operation at the earliest possible day, and the importance of bringing it into operation as soon as possible is the justification for a departure from What has been the policy of all governments in this country for the last twenty years. It does not establish any precedent, because it is definitely tied up to war needs.

In this debate on the second reading I do not propose to do more than offer a few remarks with regard to the principle of the measure. In the committee stage we can obtain further information on details and express further opinions.
When this matter came before the house on the first reading of the bill, we had the advantage of the brief remarks which the minister made on that occasion, and I suppose the memories of others than myself went back to the controversial times of ten and twelve and fifteen years ago, when a matter akin to this was a very debatable question in this house.
It is unfortunate, in my opinion, that a matter of such importance in principle and theory as this is, should have been delayed until so close to the adjournment of the house. It is a pity also, I think, that it was not sent to a committee by which all the necessary plans and documents could have been studied. As an instance, I read in the explanatory note that there is to be the diversion of a branch of a certain river, and I have been at a little pains to clarify my mind with regard to what that amounts to, lest it be

Alberta Natural Resources
the diversion of a river from another watershed into this watershed-which is always a matter of very great controversy.
I find, however, that the Ghost river is one which has several branches-shall I call them- at the tips of the fingers, up in the watershed; that this is the diversion of but one of these many branches; that in freshet time it is not an undesirable thing to relieve that piece of the mountains from freshet water, because the main Ghost river is what we in the mountains call a wicked river. It is diverted, therefore, and the water which is carried into it is diverted into lake Minnewanka. The Ghost river itself enters the Bow river below the two present developments for hydro-electric power on the Bow river, but this quantity of water will in future pass through the works at Minnewanka and then enter the Bow river, so that it can again pass through the two developments on the Bow river-which is an advantage that is understandable when explained.
But the minister has laid a good deal of emphasis on the fact that the government's decision was arrived at because of the intrusion of war necessity. I can well understand the anxiety of the Department of Munitions and Supply and that portion of the government and its officials that are intensely interested in everything which can assist the war effort. We all are, to an extent. But we must not shut our eyes to the fact that the war part of this argument is an intrusion into the larger question: shall such developments as these in the national parks be permitted? It was round that question that the controversy arose twelve years ago, and it is still a question on which there can be very wide diversity of opinion.
I am one of those who consider that the parks having been set aside for the very proper purposes of entertainment and rest, nothing should be done to impair their uses for those purposes. with regard to that dreadful strip all round this lake which lies between actual high water and what may be termed mean high water. Stumps have been removed and the clearing of debris leaves the strand, shall I call it, not unlike a sea beach.

speechtext:
I place the onus in this matter squarely on the government. How does it come about that this bill, which was introduced and given first reading on April 7, now comes for second reading on June 4, a few hours before adjournment? The responsibility is on the government and not on the opposition if the session is prolonged a day beyond this week.
The Calgary Power company has been a menace to Canada. It is just as bad as or worse than Beauharnois. I will explain why. This company came into the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec and grabbed water power at Chats falls upon which the Ontario gov-erment had to take over power. The company started in 1912. It was incorporated not by act of parliament but by a charter under the laws of Alberta, and then came down here, and got a Quebec charter to develop on the Ottawa river at Chats falls in 1926.
Who are these people? They are some of the very same people, the Montreal people, some of them behind the Sun Life, behind the Beauharnois deal, part and parcel of the super power trust. Mr. Killam was one of them, the man who owned the Mail and Empire and sold it in a merger of two newspapers in Toronto. Where there used to be six Toronto newspapers reporting the proceedings of this house, to-day there is only one. Hardly anyone knows what happens in this chamber or what is being given away. How does it come about that this bill is introduced as a war measure in the dying days of the session? It is not a war measure. That nitrogen plant should never have been established there. They knew at the time that the Alberta government had no power and this government had no power to hand over all these great water powers to private greed for gain centred in Montreal, without this house amending the parks act.
Where are the headquarters of the Calgary Power company? According to "Houston's Financial Annual, 1940," they are at 244 St. James street west, Montreal, with an operating office in Calgary. The directors of the company are G. A. Gaherty, president; I. W. Killam, of blessed memory; R. B. Baxter; Fred C. Clarke; H. H. Parlee; S. B. Hammond, and-listen to this-H. J. Symington, K.C., the war-time power controller, if you please, who has saved only about 150,000 horsepower as a war measure by daylight saving all year and then in the morning from six to nine o'clock by domestic use of power. The saving in the result is little except for alloys for the Aluminum company. The regulation is not obeyed in some towns in new Ontario. This gentleman's name is also in another company, called Calgary power in Quebec. This is the company that started in 1926 at Chats falls on the Ottawa river, an interprovincial stream.
This same process is going on in Ontario and Quebec. The Calgary Power company went to Quebec and incorporated a company in 1926 after the notorious Sifton bills to grab all the waters of new Ontario were defeated here in the Ottawa and Georgian bay canal bills, which were talked out in this parliament by those who were then sitting in opposition. When this company found that the Sifton interests had lost these extension-grab franchises on the Ottawa river, the same people, known as the Ottawa end of the Calgary Power company deal, went to Quebec and got a charter under the name of the Ottawa Valley Power company, which was owned by the Calgary Power company exclusively. They secured incorporation under the laws of Quebec. They knew enough not to come to Queen's Park in Toronto, because by the British North America Act water powers and navigation rights, international and interprovincial, are under the control of this parliament. Having got the Ottawa Valley Power Quebec charter they also incorporated on August II, 1926, as the Chats Falls Power company under the laws of Quebec, with head office at 244 St. James street, Montreal, and the same directors as the Calgary Power company, except one. On October 22, 1930, the name was changed.
How does it come about that although we have a standing committee which deals with water powers, that private bills committee has never been called? Why is this bill made a government bill? I ask the government to withdraw this bill, to leave it over until the session is resumed, perhaps in connection with the St. Lawrence waterway. Not by the widest stretch of the imagination can this
Alberta Natural Resources

plant be opened by September 1 as the situation is at present; and if it is, they are going to sell power to private people in the district at fabulous prices and under no control whatever.
The agreement in the schedule of this bill is between the dominion government represented by the Minister of Mines and Resources and the government of Alberta. When the prairie provinces got back their natural resources in 1926 I opposed the giving over of these water powers which belong to the people of Canada unless restrictions were placed in the act, because, as I contended then on behalf of the people, these water powers should not be alienated for private greed and gain the way the central provinces were looted. There is some 42,000,000 horse-power of hydro-electric energy capable of development in this country, of which only one-seventh is developed, and part of that development is only seasonal. I want a national hydro policy for this country with power at cost. I contended then that some of these people who were grabbing water powers in the Ottawa valley and eastern Ontario and Quebec sooner or later would be rapping on the door of this parliament in a power grab, as well as in Alberta and Saskatchewan, seeking to get away from the protective provisions of the National Parks Act.
I do not believe we should part with these resources as a war measure, because this is not a war measure. The plant never should have been there. The power is to be granted in perpetuity. The huge cost of our war effort has been greatly enhanced by this way of doing business. Here a nitrogen plant has been located in the Calgary district; a string of air force training camps has been built across Canada, each requiring sewage and water services furnished at fabulous cost because of wrong locations. The same principle is being followed in this bill, and it all adds to the cost of the war. Where is the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) this morning? Why was this plant located where it is? Where is the cabinet minister representing the province of Alberta? Did these two hon. gentlemen recommend this bill, this parting with power rights forever, unregulated? I doubt it very much.
We must look into the history of this company to understand what is behind this application. This bill contains only two short clauses, one validating the agreement which is set out under the schedule "A" attached to the bill, and giving the minister authority to grant the licence referred to in the agreement, notwithstanding the provisions of the National Parks Act, which is chapter 33 of

the statutes of 1930. The explanatory note states:
In 1912 the Calgary Power Company was given the right to construct a dam at the outlet of lake Minnewanka in Banff national park with right to store 44,000 acre feet of water. Following the decision to erect a nitrogen plant at Calgary for war purposes the company in November, 1940-
Away back in November of last year the government knew legislation would be required in order to get around the parks act, yet not one word was said about it until the first reading on April 7, 1941. Paragraph (e) of the agreement in schedule "A" gives the company the right to sell electric power to residents of Banff and vicinity for commercial and domestic lighting. Why, the rates will be so high that the local people will not be able to buy power at all. We had an experience with these Calgary power people in the Chaits falls development, not far from this city, and that experience should make us think twice before we pass this bill in the dying hours of the session. The policy of hon. members of the New Democracy group, who are not here in very large numbers this morning, should be "no surrender." They and the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation stand for the preservation of our water powers for the benefit of the people; they are in favour of public ownership, and I give them credit for that. I would ask them to study this bill, study the history of this company in Ontario and Quebec from 1912 on and of the power ring that had Ontario by the throat.
There is a forward move of aggression by not only this company, from 1926, on, in Alberta, and elsewhere, but we know the history of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power company, and we also know the record and history of the notorious Beauhamois company, and its subsidiaries, and interlocked directorate set-up. The great super power trust of north America never rests; it is ever on the march.
There is also, again, the Stormont Power company; I can tell hon. gentlemen that this is owned and connected1 with the Sun Life company, and that company's quasi power investments and the power campaigns, past and present, of that company in many deals at control. Recently in this house a question was asked by me in regard: to the Stormont power plant, and, as I say, it was revealed that this plant is completely owned by the Sun Life company, one of whose employees, Mr. Lawrence Jack of Montreal, now is writing articles for this wonderful publication Saturday Night to tax public utilities which operate at cost. I think it would be better on this power matter to change the name to Montreal Saturday Night for such Sun Life articles, if

Alberta Natural Resources
it is going to discuss the natural resources of this country and tax Ontario's light and power and transportation services. It is not hard to see what is being done in this connection by the old power people in Montreal. Here we have a forward movement in Alberta; there is a forward publicity movement by the Sun Life to destroy public ownership, and it is going on all across the country. No surrender, I say, to these people here. Then the explanatory note continues:
. . . the company . . . applied for permission to increase the water storage capacity to 200,000 acre feet and to construct and operate a hydroelectric plant in the park for the operation of the nitrogen plant.
As the plans of the power company to develop such additional storage involved the diversion of waters outside the park boundaries and as the park was situated within Alberta, the application was submitted to the provincial government who approved of it being granted. The national resources transfer agreement does not contemplate developments of this nature being permitted in national parks and it was deemed advisable to enter into the formal agreement referred to in the schedule hereto.
As it was planned to have the plant of the nitrogen company ready for operation on September 1, 1941, it was therefore of the utmost importance that an adequate supply of electric power be available as soon as possible. To prevent delay in completing the power expansion work, tentative permission was given to the power company under the War Measures Act to commence construction pending and subject to approval by parliament and the Alberta legislature.
You can see how the War Measures Act is sometimes twisted, broken in a racket and extended for the benefit of private greed and gain; but when it comes to erecting a small annex, needed so badly for real war work, to a technical school in Toronto, costing not more than $150,000, in order to train men for the air force and aircraft munitions, what a different story is told.
I am absolutely opposed to this proposal. I will give just one instance of what this company did in Ontario, in order that the people of Alberta may be warned, I am not responsible for taking up the time of the house; far from it. At this time blame the government. The government is to blame for trying to force this bill through the house in the dying hours of the session, without any plans or information or any regard to the opinions of those representing the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. We know these power people in Ontario; we have learned) something about their methods and how they go about getting things through this parliament, as they have for nearly thirty years in the past. Some of the millionaires who are at the head of this super power trust centred in Montreal know no politics; they are heard of at election time; they are millionaires first, last and all the time, grabbing the public domain. Now, under the War Measures Act, they are seeking to grab in perpetuity these natural resources which will be so badly needed after the war when unemployment again may have to be faced and high power rates will ruin Alberta as it will new Ontario. Then the price of coal will be so high that we shall not be able to buy any in this country. As a result industry will be starved and people will have to pay prohibitive prices for power.
What did this same company do in Ontario? I quote from page 304 of Houston's "Annual Financial Review" for 1940:
The Ottawa Valley Power Company, incorporated under the laws of Quebec, holds in part through ownership and in part by a lease from the government of the province of Quebec extending for seventy-five years from March 1, 1926, all the water power rights in the province of Quebec .at Chats Falls, on the Ottawa river.
The Ottawa river is an initerprovinoial stream, you see.
The Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario, through lease from the government of the province of Ontario, holds all the water power rights in the province of Ontario at the same site. The company and the commission have agreed that each is entitled to one-half of the water available for power, and, under a joint development agreement, there has been constructed a dam with capacity of 224,000 horse power-
That is about the same horse power involved in this bill.
[DOT]-consisting of eight units of 28,000 horse power each, four of which are owned by the company and four by the commission. One-half the total installation was completed and placed in commercial operation in 1931, and the balance in 1932. The dam and power house are owned or held on the Quebec side by the company, and on the Ontario side by the commission and, under the terms of the joint development agreement, which extends for seventy-five years from March 1, 1926, must be used jointly for the purposes of the development.
And then there was a contemplated power shortage in the province of Ontario. If you will look at the last financial statement of the Calgary Power company, which appears at page 301 of this same volume, you will see that the total assets in 1939 amounted to $25,638,014 as against $25,360,687 in 1938, and they had a large surplus as well. The consolidated income account shows gross earnings of $2,173,613 in 1939, with operating expenses of $705,108 and net operating earnings of $1,468,505. In 1938 the gross earnings were $2,114,021,. and the net operation earnings were $1,357,582. In 1937 the gross earnings were $1,998,058, and the net operation earnings $1,288,151.

When the house rose at one o'clock I had made reference to the control which the Calgary Power company was getting over electrical power resources all over Canada, and I think the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) was quite right in cautioning the house as to the dangers which might lie ahead. I have in mind the high rates for electrical power which are now being charged in the province of Alberta. In the city of Calgary, for instance, the consumer has to pay five cents per kilowatt hour. Out in the town in which I live we are paying eight cents per kilowatt hour, and in addition a seventy-cent meter charge. In the town in which I formerly lived the rate was ten cents per kilowatt hour and I believe still is, with an additional meter charge of 81.50. So that the hon. member for Broadview had reason to caution the house as to the control over the electric power generated in Canada which is being exercised by the Beauharnois company, of which company Calgary Power is a subsidiary. But I am not so much concerned about that just now, because if I understood the minister aright the province of Alberta will have control over the rates charged by Calgary Power through the public utilities commission.
What I am immediately concerned about now is making the power available because it is so urgently needed, and for that reason I am fully in accord with the step which the government has taken. I think that the Calgary Power company is to be commended for having decided to build this dam at lake Minnewanka, yet I feel it is going to be well-14873-220
paid for it. The fact remains that despite the great need in Canada, especially western Canada, for electric power, this government has consistently and persistently refused to do anything to increase the number of hydro plants to generate electricity, and the only way in which Canada could get this plant built to supply power in this great war emergency was by letting a private company do the work. The government absolutely refused to do anything about the matter itself, and it is to be condemned, I think, for that attitude, particularly when the need for power is so great. We need electric power in Alberta for the ammonium plant and for the rolling mills at Calgary. Yet the government absolutely refuses to do anything on its own behalf, advancing as its only reason, of course, that it did not have any money. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) not so long ago said that anything that was physically possible would be made financially possible in order to win the war, yet despite that declaration, the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) consistently took the stand that there was no money and that no matter how great the need might be, the government had no intention of financing the building of any dams. He brought that out clearly a while ago when he referred to the Spring lake project. He said there was a possible chance of developing a dam there, but the company had no money, and because of the lack of money we did not get the plant built and our war effort was hindered to that extent. That is the stand which the government has been taking right along.
I come back to the reasons why this dam at lake Minnewanka is being built. The government did not start this thing by itself at all, as the minister would lead us to believe. A committee of all the Alberta members became interested in this project, and as a result the minister acted, and I think he did the proper thing when he decided to go ahead and build this project at l ike Minnewanka. But the fact is that now the power is there. It is not even necessary to wait for it to be developed at lake Minnewanka. Because of the Calgary Power company's plant on Ghost river, they could use immediately the reservoir of water they have there to increase their supply of electric power, because, as I am informed upon good authority, they would have this fall, when they need it, the extra supply coming from lake Minnewanka. The unfortunate part of it is that now that we are in a position to have abundance of electrical energy there, the Calgary rolling mill is being taken out of that district and removed to Vancouver. That is a very serious mistake, not because the mill was originally in Calgary, but because, in view of the fact that we are at war, it should be opened in Calgary immediately. There is going to be considerable delay in transferring the mill from Calgary to Vancouver, not to speak of the cost entailed in the shipment of the equipment. If we need the steel, steps should be taken to start operations right where the plant is. If we do not need steel, that is a different matter, but the government has not intimated that there is any overabundance of steel.
Is there any reason why that electric power should not be used in the Calgary rolling mill immediately? I am informed that the present freight rates on scrap iron, Whether moved east or west, are almost prohibitive-and freight rates are always going up instead of coming down. That should be a deciding factor in the production of this steel. Then comes the handling of this scrap iron. I am informed by reliable men in this

business that a tremendous amount of work is required to prepare scrap iron for shipment either west or east of the prairie provinces. The obvious and most sensible thing at this time is to have scrap iron sent into Calgary, worked over there into steel plates or rods, and shipped, if necessary, to Vancouver. The rate would be less, and fewer cars would be required. I am informed that there are immediately available in Calgary over 200,000 tons of scrap. We could start producing steel at once in Calgary; we would not have to wait for the company to move its plant to Vancouver, which will entail three or four or five months' delay.
There remains the problem of labour. The minister may say that insufficiency of labour is one of the chief reasons why this plant should be moved from Calgary to the coast. But there are in the prairie provinces hundreds of physically fit men, unemployed, who could immediately be put to this work. He may say that they are not trained, but training is a matter of only a week or so; as a matter of fact, many of these men are skilled in industry and are wondering why, during war time, they cannot get jobs. Well they might ask that question, when we are supposed to be engaged in an all-out war effort-that term Which is so much misused. There will come a time when these skilled men will drift to other places, and then the minister may have cause to complain that labour cannot be obtained. If we are serious in this matter, immediate action should be taken.
I have a letter from the Canadian Junk company, in which, referring to this very matter, they give three reasons, which seem to me sound, why this electric power should be used to open the Calgary rolling mill. They say:
Firstly, the expense of moving the mill would be avoided.
If I am not mistaken, the minister mentioned a while ago that there would be a certain amount of depreciation over a period of about two years, which this company would write off, relative to the cost of moving this equipment.
Secondly, there is the availability of cheap natural gas. Millions of dollars' worth of this gas is still being wasted, even with present regulations in Turner valley. Eastern steel mills obtain cheap fuel by using by-product coke oven gas. We are not aware that this method is possible at the coast.
Thirdly, scap steel can be landed at Calgary cheaper than at the coast. Fewer freight cars will be required,-
I think that is an essential point.

as the finished product is less bulky than scrap steel, and there is a certain amount of shrinkage, due to manufacture.

Alberta Natural Resources
The matter of shrinkage is important when one figures the excess freight rate which would have to be paid.
I cannot see any logical reason why the Calgary rolling mill should not be opened now and all the steel made which it is possible to make. That is one of the reasons why I believe it is high time that the project at lake Minnewanka Should be developed and power produced as cheaply as possible. I hope the government will reconsider allowing the Dominion Bridge company to move these rolling mills from Calgary to Vancouver, because it will cause long and unnecessary delay in the manufacture of the steel which is now so greatly needed.

subtopic: AGREEMENT RESPECTING POWER DEVELOPMENT FOR WAR PURPOSES AFFECTING WATERS IN BANFF NATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that I must rise to add some support to the case made so well this morning by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). In my opinion he made it very clear that this bill is quite unnecessary. The government, under the War Measures Act, has all the powers necessary to develop all the power potential at any place in Canada. I want to protest against the passing of special legislation which will give to the Calgary Power company the benefits which this legislation will, in my opinion, confer.
According to "Poor's Financial Records, 1940," this is a company which already has a very large control of power in western Canada. It was incorporated in 1909, under the laws of the Dominion of Canada. I quote:
The company holds, in the province of Alberta, under licence from the government, all the water power of the Bow river at Horseshoe falls and Kananaskis falls, and the right to store water at lake Minnewanka, all for four periods of 21 years each, and all the water power at the Ghost-Radnor site, and the right to store water at Upper Kananaskis lake, both for a period of 50 years.
The company has, since 1911, been engaged in the production and sale of electricity in the province of Alberta. Three-quarters of the electricity generated in the province is produced by the company's water power plants. Its 2,500-mile transmission system extends over a large part of the more thickly settled area of the province, serving a quarter of a million people. From a point 40 miles north of Edmonton, it extends southward to within^ a few miles of the international boundary, with a main lateral branch reaching east to the Saskatchewan boundary,
In Alberta, serves 15,357 retail customers over its own distribution lines, and, in addition, supplies the entire power requirements of the municipal distribution systems of Calgary, Red Deer, Maeleod, Cardston and Ponoka, and also most of the power used in a number of towns and villages on the system of Canadian Utilities Limited. Power is sold direct to the Exshaw plant of Canada Cement Company Limited, to coal mines and to a number of other industries. Company's lines also serve the Turner valley oi,l fields. An interchange agreement is in effect with East Kootenay Power Company Limited.
During 1937, a new agreement was executed with the city of Calgary covering its power requirements for a further period of ten years from the expiration of the existing contract on July 31, 1940. The other wholesale agreements are for varying periods, and the distribution franchises are for the maximum periods allowed under the laws of the province.
Company controls, through a wholly-owned sub,. Prairie Power Company Limited, a modern system in Saskatchewan, comprising 180 miles of transmission lines, with distribution systems serving 2,810 retail customers. Power for operations of the systems of the Saskatchewan Power Commission and of Canadian Utilities Limited, is also transmitted over the lines of that company.
The explanatory note reads:
To prevent delay in completing the power expansion works, tentative permission was given to the power company under the War Measures Act to commence construction pending and subject to approval by parliament and the Alberta legislature.

subtopic: AGREEMENT RESPECTING POWER DEVELOPMENT FOR WAR PURPOSES AFFECTING WATERS IN BANFF NATIONAL PARK
speechtext: It is quite true that under the War Measures Act this work could be undertaken, but any authority under the War Measures Act lapses with the end of war and the conclusion of peace; consequently it is necessary to have authority by parliament to make it permanent and continuous.

speechtext: That is the very point I am complaining about. This parliament under the stress of war, when everyone is anxious that war production should be carried on as efficiently as possible, should not hand over to the Calgary Power company for all time the privileges in question.

speechtext: That is not what you were saying.

subtopic: AGREEMENT RESPECTING POWER DEVELOPMENT FOR WAR PURPOSES AFFECTING WATERS IN BANFF NATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
That is what I am protesting against. We can complete all the necessary power development at the present time and when the war is over make arrangements with the Calgary Power company for the disposition of this particular utility. I submit that the history of power companies in Canada is such that hon. members have reason to be suspicious of these corporations who come to parliament and ask for such consideration as the Calgary Power company is now seeking. As the hon. member for Broadview pointed out, one of the directors of the company, H. J. Symington, is one of the dollar-a-year men in Canada, as indicated in the latest list received from the Department of National War Services, and he is the power representative on the war-time industries control board. With one of the directors of this company occupying a key position on the war-time industries control board, it would be much better for this company to wait until the war is over before Coming to parliament and asking that consideration, which might be all right in peace time, be extended
Alberta Natural Resources

to the company to make available to them benefits which will undoubtedly accrue for all time.
In the Winnipeg Free Press of November 25 there was an article from which I quote:
The Calgary Power company has applied for the right to convert lake Minnewanka in Banff national park into a storage basin and to develop hydro electric power from it at a nearby point. The reason given for the application is that the company is being asked to supply power to a new war chemicals plant in southern Alberta and that the needs of this plant will impair the company's power reserve.
Hon. members are most anxious that Alberta should have chemical plants and rolling mills and that every able-bodied person in that province should be working during the war period; and if additional power is necessary it should by all means be granted under the War Measures Act. But the time of this parliament should not be occupied in dealing with legislation such as this bill in behalf of the Calgary Power company.
According to a brief presented by the Federation of Ontario Naturalists, in January, 1941, it is said that this is not the first time that the Calgary Power company has asked for consideration of this sort. I read:
Prior to 1923, the company, with powerful support from city councils and boards of trade in southern Alberta, put on a drive to convert lake Minnewanka into a storage basin. The water was to be fed into the Bow river and would pass through the company's power plants at Calgary. The application, pressed vigorously prior to 1923, failed to succeed for the reason that lake Minnewanka is one of the loveliest lakes in Banff national park and the government of the day refused to permit the beauty of the park to be defaced by concrete dams and muddy waterless shorelines. The haring of wide stretches of shoreline is inevitable in a power storage development; the very purpose of storage makes wide fluctuations in the water level essential.
I am not pressing the point put forward by the naturalists, who are concerned about the beauty spots in Banff national park. I agree with those who drafted the brief that the lake is one of the most beautiful anywhere in the Rocky mountains, or in the world for that matter; but in time of war those who prize these natural beauty spots must be prepared to see them sacrificed if power is necessary. Granting that, however, it does not follow that those who are interested financially in the Calgary Power company should take advantage of the present crisis to obtain in war time what they could not get in peace time. When the war is over, I repeat, when we finish with Hitler, it will be soon enough to determine the financial arrangements that will be necessary with the Calgary Power company as a result of the
IMr. Nicholson.1
developments they will find essential to supply the power needed in our war industries. This
brief states:
The government, under the War Measures Act, could authorize the development at Minnewanka by order in council-setting aside the National Parks Act-but it is understood this would be unsatisfactory to the company. When the war ends, the War Measures Act no longer operates, and the National Parks Act will at once come into play. Any development carried out under the War Measures Act, therefore, would be without statutory sanction in peace time. The company, it is believed, insists that special statute be enacted permanently authorizing the lake Minnewanka development.
I add my protest as forcibly as I can to the one made by the hon. member for Broadview. Taking into consideration the importance of the many other items that should be considered, and in view of the fact that not one single horse-power more of electricity will be developed by the passing of this measure, I ask the minister to reconsider the bill and let it stand until the war has been won.

subtopic: AGREEMENT RESPECTING POWER DEVELOPMENT FOR WAR PURPOSES AFFECTING WATERS IN BANFF NATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
I should be remiss in my duty to my constituency and to the country if I did not say something in connection with this bill, inasmuch as the power project under discussion is wholly within the constituency which I represent, Calgary West.
At the outset I may say that no one should be more concerned about exploring all the considerations which have agitated the minds of hon. members than myself as the representative of those people. Certainly no people in any part of Canada are or should be more zealous to preserve the beauties of our national parks, because they not only enjoy the beauties of this locality but gain their livelihood from the visitors who come from all parts of the world to see the beauty spots of our Rockies. Yet it is a surprising thing that without exception I have received no word of protest in regard to this proposal from any of the people of Calgary West, which embraces Banff, Lake Louise and West Calgary. As a matter of fact the Banff advisory council, under date of November 27 last, wrote me a letter which I should like to read, showing what these people have to say with regard to this matter. The letter is addressed to me, signed by Mr. R. E. W. Edwards, secretary of the Banff advisory council, who by the way is in no way related to me. It reads:
Dear Sir:-
I am enclosing herewith a copy of a telegram sent last night to the hon. the Minister of National Defence.
The feeling in Banff is that no considerations should be allowed to interfere with the production of invaluable war material in the present crisis, especially as this project will enable production to be carried on at a minimum cost.

Alberta Natural Resources
Also the existence of a plant capable of supplying almost unlimited power at low cost will be undoubtedly a great factor in the establishment of many new industries in the province of Alberta on the conclusion of the war and will prove a tremendous asset to the wealth of the province.
The raising of the level of the lake will do away with certain unsightly features which at present exist in the neighbourhood of the lake and render it more attractive than ever to the travelling public, and, finally, this scheme will provide decent employment for a large number of men who otherwise will, with their dependents, suffer much hardship during the winter months owing to lack of suitable work.
For these and other reasons, equally potent, which will suggest themselves to you, the advisory council ask that you do everything in your power to aid in procuring authorization for the carrying out of the Calgary Power Company's project as there can be no doubt that, both now and in the years to come, it will prove of inestimable benefit to the national park and to Alberta as a whole.
I have received similar communications from the Banff board of trade, the Calgary board of trade and numerous other bodies. I can truthfully say that I have not received any letter of protest or opposition to this proposal from any resident of West Calgary.

They are thousands of miles away, nevertheless. Let us be fair about this. I have talked with a number of people who object on principle to impounding water anywhere or making any economic use of the gifts of the Almighty. But after all we live in an industrial and power age; society must go on. I have not 'had the privilege of travelling on the continent of Europe, but when one thinks of an industrialized country, Switzerland is immediately suggested. Switzerland is world famous for its mountain beauty and also for its industrial development. I am informed1 that all the lakes and rivers in Switzerland have their waters impounded for power development, and the success of Switzerland as an industrial nation is dependent upon its water power. If it is true, as I believe it to be, that the waters of lake Minnewanka, which ordinarily in the spring run down into Bow river and off to the sea in a headlong rush, serving no useful purpose so far as power is concerned, can be stored so that they run down during the season when power is most needed, then I think that should be done.

speechtext:
The result of the construction of this dam will be to store water in lake Minnewanka where already, as the minister has pointed out, there is some storage of water. The dam will increase the amount of water stored there during the season when there is a heavy run-off, so that it may be used in the fall and winter when otherwise there would be a shortage of water for power purposes. It must be borne in mind that the water will be used at the Minnewanka plant; then it will go down the Bow river to the Kananaskis plant, where it will generate power; then it will go farther down the river to the Horseshoe plant, where it will generate more power, and then on down the river to the Ghost river plant, where it will generate still more power. In other words the waters stored by this dam will be used four times, and that is the fact that makes this a sound proposition. The last three plants named-the Ghost, Horseshoe and Kananaskis plants-are all outside the park area.
There is one other aspect of the matter to which I should like to refer. I became somewhat exercised when I learned that the government was considering the establishment of an ammonium nitrate or chemical plant in western Canada. I was told that the manufacture of ammonium nitrate under modern chemical practice required the compression of natural gas and air, and when I contemplate the millions of cubic feet of natural gas that have been going to waste in the Turner valley for at least twenty years, to my own knowledge, it seemed to me that there was only one logical and economical place where that plant should be erected, namely, at Calgary. But in addition to the gas, air and water, power is required. It is my understanding that the

operation of this plant will require some 23,000 horse-power, and that power will have to be supplied continuously, night and day. There will not be high peaks and low ebbs as is ordinarily the case in commercial plants; there will be a steady drain on the power resources of that district, and the question was how that power should be obtained. There were other alternatives, to which reference has been made; there were the Kananaskis proposition and the Spray lakes development, which would have involved expenditures many times greater than those contemplated under this project, with the further objection that the power would not have been so readily available. It is contemplated that this plant, which is now almost completed, will be in operation this fall, that this plant at Minnewanka, operated by the Calgary Bower company, will have power available for the operation of the plant at that time. Under this project power will be made available more cheaply than it could under any other scheme, and in addition no capital outlay is involved on the part of the Canadian people.
One other consideration which to me is cogent and convincing is that this project has the unanimous endorsation of the government of Alberta, who I am sure would be most jealous and zealous in protecting the rights of the people of that province. Certainly no one could accuse the government of Alberta of being unduly anxious to place themselves or the people of that province in the hands-or the maw, if you will-of the financial interests of St. James Street or anywhere else. Further, I am reliably informed that this company is in no way connected with or a subsidiary of the so-called Beauharnois Power Corporation. I am not concerned with that, however; I hope we may deal with this matter on its own merits. The province of Alberta, through its public utilities board, has absolute control over the rate structure of all public utilities in the province; and I am sure it will deal fairly but justly with the Calgary Power company should any attempt be made to take advantage of the people of Alberta in the matter of rates. I am not in the least agitated or exercised over the ability of the province of Alberta to look after itself so far as rates are concerned. Neither am I disturbed or alarmed as to the scenic beauties of lake Minnewanka. My personal opinion is that those scenic beauties will be enhanced, if anything, as a result of this improvement.
The other point about which I am concerned is the post-war value of this project, in common with that of all other war projects. This will entail no headache to the Canadian people; it is not an enterprise that will be pawned off

for its salvage value. I see in this a stepping stone to the development of another economic centre for the Dominion of Canada. The province of Alberta is singularly blessed with natural resources such as coal, gas, oil, timber and other gifts of the Almighty, which are there to be developed. But, as the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) has pointed out, we the people of Alberta realize that the corner stone of economic and industrial development is power-an abundance of power. The Minister of Munitions and Supply has emphasized that point. Here is a possibility of making available surplus power for industrial development following the war.	.
For these reasons I know my constituents are whole-heartedly behind the _ bill before the house, and are anxious that it should be proceeded with.

speechtext:
Let me be the first to wave those suggestions to one side, in the interests of Canada. When I think of Canada's interests in this connection I think of what was in the mind of the hon. member who said that Alberta was blessed with natural resources of a kind which perhaps are not found to the same degree in other parts of Canada. I am thinking now, while the war is on, of the ammonium salts of all kinds, of the nitrates and the ammonium nitrates which can be produced from the natural resources of Alberta, and which are so much required at
this time of war. I would waive all other considerations if I were sure that this legislation would increase the production of those vital necessities of war. I refer of course to ammonium salts and nitrates. We need them. Whether they come from the coal of Alberta, or from the nitrates and ammoniates reclaimed from the gases which come from the oil wells of the Turner valley-no matter whence they come, we need them. We in this chamber should address ourselves more and more to the task of accumulating in order to supply to our forces the chemical necessities of war. If this legislation is purely a war measure, as was intimated some months ago when the matter was first placed before us, and which has been again emphasized-then, yes, by all means let us support this legislation.
At the same time many of us are supporters of public ownership, and we are a little sceptical of what an hon. member has described as St. James street, Montreal, and Bay street, Toronto. We are public ownership men, but even if we have to put to one side our public ownership ideas and let private ownership come forward, with all its enterprise, intuition and forcefulness to develop this power, in order that through that power there may be developed more and more war supplies, then by all means let us go ahead with this legislation, and let the hon. member from the constituency affected, together with his associates, attend to their task of developing this power. Let them see to it that the power, in turn, is used to produce more and more war supplies.
I did not very much like the interruption to the effect that some of us live a thousand miles away from the scene where this development is taking place.

speechtext: The hon. member for Calgary West made that suggestion.

speechtext:
It was suggested that that was one reason why we should not make interjections when a subject of this magnitude is under consideration. My answer is that we are Canadians, and as such we think of Canada' from Halifax to Vancouver. And, in greater particularity, we are thinking of war conditions. Possibly we are not thinking just enough about the fact that the empire is at war. These picayune interruptions might very well be left to one side when we are discussing a problem of the magnitude of the one now under consideration.
So I say, Mr. Speaker, that if this project, whether operated under private or public ownership, is going to help in any way whatsoever in our war effort, by all means let us get on with it. Let us produce the power, so that that power may produce more nitrates
Alberta Natural Resources

and. ammoniates from the gases, coal and oils of the Turner valley. Let us produce from the coal of Alberta. Let us help out in this war effort in every possible way.
When the war is over the prairie provinces will need more ammoniates; they will need more nitrates after the last two decades of mining the prairie provinces. Because that observation comes from Ontario some of my western friends may not like it, but they know in their own hearts that crop after crop was taken off and no return was made to the soil. Protein crops have been harvested in western Canada. Here is a project which, if developed, will produce and return to t'he soil the protein value which has been taken from it in the last two or three decades. The Consolidated Mining and Smelting company spent a couple of million dollars at Trail, British Columbia, to recover the fertilizing value of the gases escaping from their stacks. They had in mind not only the fact that they were disposing of a nuisance to municipalities south of the boundary line and in Canada, but also the fact that those same gases had fertilizer value. The gases were therefore trapped and transmuted into salts which could be used as fertilizers. I do not know how many millions of dollars were spent, but the company did tackle the problem of saving the ammoniates and nitrates from the stacks of its gigantic plant at Trail. The scientific research carried on at the Trail plant has rendered a great service to Canada. It may be that the company was thinking ahead to the time When they might sell the fertilizing product to the western farmers.
The project we are considering to-day will twin up, as it were, with the development at Trail, and help to reestablish in western Canada lands which will again produce bushel-age equal to that produced from those virgin soils twenty or thirty years ago. Let us keep in mind the fact that the Canadian people are public-ownership minded. We do mot like to hear mention of St. James street, Montreal; we do not like to hear about Bay street, Toronto, because in this chamber for twenty years their tactics ahd ways of conducting business have been denounced. This is or seems to be a child of organizations of that kind. My hon. friend Shakes his head. That makes me feel a little better about it, and if that should be the situation, I say to the hon. member for Calgary and those charged with the passage of this legislation, by all means let us give consideration to its passing. Let us have the power, let us have the nitrates, let us have the ammoniates and what-not. Let us one and all in this chamber address ourselves to the great task that is before us, namely, the winning of the war.

I think it is safe to say that if the war feature were not in this proposal the minister would have had the very greatest hesitation in bringing forward legislation of this kind.
