subtopic: AGREEMENT RESPECTING POWER DEVELOPMENT FOR WAR PURPOSES AFFECTING WATERS IN BANFF NATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
I accept that statement without reserve. It is because of the war feature that I am disposed to give support to the measure. If it is represented to us in this house by those in a position of responsibility that this proposal, which is merely the extension of a principle which has already been adopted, namely, the harnessing of the powers of the Bow river, will in any measurable degree help win this war, I do not think we should hesitate very long about debating it. After all, let us be realistic; let us be honest with ourselves. We are always declaring that what matters most at the moment is the winning of the war. I myself have taken that attitude on many occasions. But I suggest to the minister that he should have brought this measure forward earlier in the session so that hon. members would have had more time to study it and know exactly its implications.
I think I should say a word about the sponsors of this power proposition. They are an old established power company in Canada, in the business for gain; there is no question about that. But they are engaged in a legitimate business, a business which has been recognized over a long period of years, and so far as I am aware-and I think I am aware of the facts-they are not in any way connected with the so-called Beauhamois interests-that is, Montreal Light, Heat and Power. It cannot be said, therefore, that they are in furtherance of a particular power monopoly in Canada. But even if they were connected with Montreal power interests I

Alberta Natural Resources
do not think that would be a factor in influencing me at the moment in connection with this measure or in weighing, pro and con, the arguments in favour of or against it. Suffice it to say that these interests have been in the Bow river valley and1 in that district now for a period approaching forty years.
I am not aware whether the proposal for this development was made to the power company by the officers of the crown, the department of munitions, or whether the position was the reverse, and I do not think it matters very much. I have no manner of doubt that the Calgary Bower company, taking the broad and long view of the situation, has wanted to get this storage over a long period of time. Perhaps it is true, as has been stated, that in 1923 offers were made by the company with a view to securing increased storage at this site, lake Minne-wanka. That I do not think is a vital question at the moment. The vital thing is this: is the government in concurring in this proposal helping the war effort? In so doing is it injuring, first of all, the national park at Banff, and, secondly, is it violating any great principle? If the whole power proposition in that region were being approached for the first time, other considerations might prevail. The doctrine of public ownership might prevail, although I do not know Whether it would or not. I cannot subscribe, with my colleague from Danforth (Mr. Harris), to the principle of public ownership. I am not a public ownership man. I want to preach the doctrine in this house, and I have preached it before, of private enterprise in ordinary times. I do not, therefore, base on either principle any remarks I may have to make in connection with this proposal.
If it is established' to the satisfaction of the government and of the minister and of the department that this development is necessary in connection with the war, then, whatever hesitation I may have from any other point of view, I think I should support the measure. The difficulty is just this. The capital cost of the proposed development is so great that no company would be justified in asking its shareholders or its creditors- and it must get the money from either of these two sources-to put up the necessary capital for an enterprise that was intended purely for the duration of the war. I am satisfied that the Calgary Power company or any other business concern would never consider this development purely as a war project and a war project only, and for the duration only. It just would not be business. In that event what would the company do? It would come to the government and say: 14873-221
"We will develop this power, but at your capital cost". That has been done on many occasions in this war. The government has done it very extensively, and I have often wondered whether it was justified in going as far as it has gone. I have not been able to investigate the different avenues in which they have taken that course, but I do know that the capital commitments of the country in that respect have been very great. But I have no doubt that the Minister of Munitions and Supply and members of the government charged with the responsibility will justify every capital expenditure on the building of government-owned plants on the ground of necessity for war purposes, although they are plants which would not be established by any private enterprise during the war unless it were fully compensated or had guarantees of compensation to absorb capital loss if in the meantime money was not made out of the operation of the plant.
This company asks as a condition precedent that, in consideration of putting up the two million odd dollars in capital for development of proposed storage, it be given this right for a long period of time, you might say in effect in perpetuity. Of course that must have created for the minister and for the department a substantial difficulty. It raises a question in my own mind of balancing the good resulting from the franchise, in the expenditure of money for this purpose during the war, against what is practically an extension of their franchise in perpetuity. I am not in a position, with the limited information at my hand, to judge as to whether the decision which the minister and the government have reached is a correct decision or not. If a matter of this sort were coming up early in the session I would want to have a bill of this character referred to some select committee to investigate, where they could hear the evidence pro and con, pass a judgment, and make a considered report to the house. That is not possible to-day. I think the minister has delayed too long proceeding with this measure.
However, in the final analysis he has decided this question in the affirmative. For that decision the minister and the ministry must take responsibility; and I assume that, by putting their imprimatur on this bill and making it a government measure, they are prepared to do so; and, because it is their responsibility, I propose to leave it there.
I would not want the house to understand that there are no implications on the other side. It is too late to turn back on this thing, even if the house were so disposed, because months ago the government gave an

Alberta Natural Resources

interim licence to this company, and I understand that the company have gone on with the work and expended already a very large sum of money on the basis of the undertaking given and of the order in council passed as long ago as December, 1940. I have no doubt that, through an informal undertaking made anterior to that, the company's work is near consummation; indeed it is stated some place, either in these papers or in the minister's statement, that the extra power which will be developed through this project will be available by September 1. If that is so it is all to the good as far as the war effort is concerned, because, make no mistake about it, the product of this plant in Calgary is needed, and will be needed more and more every day as the war progresses.
I am in no position to judge whether Calgary is the right place for the establishment of this plant. From what I have heard I should say it is admirably so adapted. If that is so, I am glad to see some government industrial establishment in the western provinces. It is something for which some of us from the smaller provinces have been contending in this house for months. We have argued that alL this new war industry should not be located in central Canada, as has been far too much the case. Only six-tenths of one per cent of all the capital expenditures made by this government on wrar industry have been allocated to New Brunswick, that little province down by the sea, where, in the last war, we made literally hundreds of thousands of shells and other war material. That is one of the causes of complaint against the government. I know the excuse is that there is lack of power; I am not quite sure that the excuse is a good one. But that is merely in passing.
Another argument against this proposal, advanced in certain quarters, is that which, if my information be correct, prompted the permanent officials of the minister's department in their first opposition to this proposal- if they did oppose it-has to do with the question of the destruction of the scenic beauties. Notwithstanding anything that the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Edwards) may have said, you cannot, generally speaking, disturb nature without some destruction of natural beauty. It is a question, then, of balance: which is the better thing to do. If you decide to disturb nature you should, so far as is humanly possible within the limits of engineering skill, minimize the destruction of natural scenic beauty. I have had the benefit of reading the draft of the proposed lease, the "interim licence" it is called, and I want to say that whoever drafted this licence took the utmost care to minimize as

far as possible the damage which will accrue to the scenic beauties of that wonderful lake which I have had the pleasure of seeing and which I hope to visit again before I die. I repeat that whoever drafted this licence took infinite pains to guard against that danger, so far as it can be guarded against by foresight, by experience and by vision. I am inclined to think that there will be very little destruction of scenic beauty, and therefore I do not believe any great body of opposition should on that ground be directed against this proposal.
I should like to point out the full extent of the rights to be conferred under the proposals now before the house. At the risk of detaining the house a few minutes I will place them on record as they appear in the form of the draft agreement between this government and the government of Alberta. The provincial government has to consent in a certain degree and with respect to certain factors before this project may become operative:
(a)	The right to raise lake Minnewanka to [DOT]a full supply level of elevation 4,840 feet above mean sea level (geodetic datum) or such lesser elevation as may subsequently be determined by the Minister of Mines and Resources as being the economic maximum with the right to store water up to said elevation and use 200,000 acre-feet of the storage so created or such lesser amount as may subsequently be determined by the said minister-
That is, the Minister of Mines and Resources.

as being the economic maximum by the construction of a dam across the Cascade River valley at or near the outlet of the said lake;
(b)	The right to divert, take and use the water so stored for power purposes by diverting the same through a canal and conduit down a lateral valley to a power station to be constructed on the Cascade River flat at or near Anthracite, and at that point to return the water by suitable works to the Cascade river:
(c)	The right to convey the waters of the Ghost river into lake Minnewanka

I assume that this is part of the scheme with which the province of Alberta is concerned:
-through a canal extending from the park boundary to lake Minnewanka;
(d)	The right to construct transmisison lines with the necessary rights-of-way connecting the proposed power station with the existing transmission system of the company outside the park and the system now supplying Banff;
(e)	The right to sell electric power to residents in Banff townsite and vicinity;
(f)	And generally the right to perform such acts in connection with said storage and power development scheme as may be approved from time to time by the Minister of Mines and Resources.
Be it borne in mind that this right is not for the duration of the war, or for to-day or to-morrow. When it is granted, when this

Alberta Natural Resources
legislation is passed, it is to be practically in perpetuity. All right. The thing is accepted; and because it is an accomplished fact, because it. is represented as being necessary in connection with the war, we should be careful about the degree of our opposition to it. I am inclined to agree with the minister that if it were not for the war aspect we ought to oppose it; yet I can see another point of view with respect to the industrial development, of that part of the province of Alberta.
War or no war, Alberta has the right, having regard to its great store of natural resources, to look forward to the day when it will be industrialized. What has been the whole effort of this country ever since I was a boy? It has been as far as possible to have an industrial life in Canada. I know there are people in this country who do not agree with that point of view. I have heard the minister himself in days gone by, right from these seats, declare that this country should encourage only those industries which are indigenous to the land. Well, we have gone a long way beyond that. If the people of Calgary have at their door great potent'nl water powers, even though they form part of the national park, even though in the natural state they constitute a great beauty, I am afraid that if I were a citizen of Calgary I would be all for the development of the natural power, whether by St. James street or by the government of Alberta. What we want is progress. Are we to be hewers of wood and drawers of water all our lives? Are the people of Alberta to be confined to the growing of wheat all their lives? Present day indications suggest that they had better try to change their whole economy. If this will have the effect of changing the economy of that part of Alberta, then I think we are justified in voting for this measure, even though we may be violating some other tenets which we hold with regard to national parks. I will vote for the measure, but I must say that I do so after a great deal of hesitation and some study of the whole situation.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata); Since it is impossible to take advantage of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to develop the water power described in the schedule to Bill No. 60, an act to amend the Alberta Natural Resources Act, I do not share the views of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). I do not say this because he has expressed them; I have other reasons. Of course everything we do, we are told, has something to do with the war. If a member blows his nose in this house we are to believe it has something to do with the war. We cannot move a step without having this said.
14873-221J
I am opposed to this legislation and perhaps the house will sit ten days longer because of contentious bills that are brought in at the last minute. This is not the way to set an example to the provincial legislatures with regard to the passing of legislation.
It will be said, in reply, that it is the will of the province of Alberta, and that is all right. But there is something deeper than that. There was drum-beating when the natural resources were transferred to the prairie provinces eleven years ago, but it was a mistake, and the mistake was made before that. The mistake was in the creation of the western provinces. It was a great mistake. They should have remained northwest territories and everyone would have been better off. But as matters stand, the three prairie provinces having been created thirty-seven years ago, the natural resources have been handed over to them, depriving the dominion government of all guarantees it had for the loans made to the provinces. An agreement was signed between the dominion government and the government of Alberta and therefore it is pretty hard now to oppose this legislation successfully. I suggest, however, that legislation should be considered objectively, and with regard to every piece of legislation brought forward every member should ask himself this question: Is it good or bad legislation? Every member should ask himself that question without considering whether it pleases Mr. So-and-So or the Hon. Mr. So-and-So, or the Hon. the Premier of Such and Such a province, et cetera, et cetera.
Here w'e are in the presence of an accomplished fact, namely, that the government will disburse $240,000 on this project. Have we the means to do it? The answer is no, and we cannot decently ask the taxpayers of Canada to pay taxes for such schemes. It is all right for a man who has money in the bank to dispose of it as he pleases, but no government has the right to deprive the taxpayers of Canada of their money in order to encourage schemes like this to favour millionaires such as those in that company. It is bad legislation. No one can argue to my satisfaction that it is good legislation. How is it that the unemployed in my county cannot receive a cent from this government? It has been cut. Yet there are millionaires who own a big power corporation at Calgary and who can get $240,000. And we say it is a war measure. That is a great excuse; it is the general excuse.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) laughs. Well, he is a laughing example of self-contradiction. Every time he rises he says, "I am against this or that," and then, "I am all for it." He has only to scratch the
Alberta Natural Resources

inside of his hand with one or two fingers and he is all for it. I should like him to be more serious, and instead of being so contradictory he should have the wisdom to remain silent and not say black and then say white, and not say white and then say black.
I regret that at this time of the session, the closing days of the session, legislation such as this should be brought forward. It will have a bad effect. If Liberal members had been asked beforehand about it they would have been wiser than the government of Alberta and would have said, "No, we cannot do it." I wonder if it is not a reminder of the last provincial election in Alberta, and if there was not an agreement between the government and the Calgary Power company at that time. And is it not on account of that promise that the provincial government was bound to sign "yes" to the exorbitant request of the power company? One has only to open his eyes to see and to look and read between the lines. It is easy to understand. It is no secret; it is on paper, and it is not only on paper but on official paper, on the official record. Are we to spend money now to refund to the Calgary Power company any election subscriptions made to the government of Alberta? That is the question.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
subtopic: AGREEMENT RESPECTING POWER DEVELOPMENT FOR WAR PURPOSES AFFECTING WATERS IN BANFF NATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
I shall detain the house only a very few minutes. The suggestion or claim has been made in the course of the debate that this is not a war measure, that there is something almost sinister behind the business of granting to the Calgary Power company the right to store water in lake Minne-wanka. Let me make it unequivocally clear that this is a war measure. If I had not been convinced that it is necessary to provide continuous power for the development of an ammonium nitrate industry very much needed for the production of munitions, I would not have made the recommendation to my colleagues that this measure be proceeded with. And I am quite sure that the government would not have approved the measure. Let there be no misunderstanding about that.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) seemed to argue on both sides of the question. I rather gathered from the remarks of the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) that he was in a somewhat similar position. The hon. member for Bow River stated that the Calgary Power company was a subsidiary of the Beauharnois company. It is not my business here to deal with either the virtues or the iniquities of power companies, but I can assure the hon. member for Bow River that there is no connection whatever between the Calgary Power company and the Beauharnois company. As

a matter of fact in their own fields in other parts of Canada I understand that there is a good deal of rivalry between them.
The hon. member for Mackenzie also made the suggestion that we should let the matter stand, that we should not proceed with this measure until the war is over. That as a practical matter is quite impossible. The outlay by the company for these works will be almost $2,400,000. Even in these days that is a considerable sum of money, and if a company asked the public or its shareholders to supply this amount of money for a development of this kind on the assumption that after the war they would get some authority to continue it, it would be impossible for them to get the money. There can be no question about that in the mind of any reasonable person who is aware of the facts. The matter is one of war emergency, and I repeat, that is the only reason it is before the house.
The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) is I think under a misapprehension, if I understood his remarks correctly. There is no proposal in this measure to pay $240,000 to the Calgary Power company or anyone associated with it. The government sells its present power plant and distribution system in the town of Banff to the Calgary Power company. That distribution system and the power plant cost $240,000, and we get from the Calgary Power company the depreciated value of the plant. The basis of arriving at the amount of depreciation has to be agreed upon between the government and the company. In addition the company pays to the government $100,000 over and above what it pays for the depreciated value of the plant, and on top of that, as I have stated, the government is assured of 500,000 kilowatt hours of electrical energy free of cost, its additional, requirements at half a cent a kilowatt hour, and the citizens of Banff are assured of their light and power requirements at rates no greater than they are paying at the present time and under conditions subject bo review by the public utilities board of Alberta when they wish to have them reviewed. In that respect I think we have effectively protected the people of the town of Banff.

He seems to argue that in the agreement we are giving wide powers to the company. Possibly the hon. member has not read the agreement very closely. For instance, in paragraph (a) to which he referred, all we do is to give the right to raise the lake level above the point to which permission was given in the agreement of 1912. We permit the company to store up to but not exceeding
200,000	acre-feet of water.
Quite obviously, if a storage reservoir were to be created by the company under these conditions, it was necessary to give it power to create the conditions which would make

Alberta Natural Resources
such storage effective. Paragraph (b) confers the right to divert, take and use the water so stored for the purpose of developing this power at or near Anthracite. That is, in the first place we give the power to store the water, and in the second place we give power to divert from storage to the power plant.
I do not think there is anything extraordinary about that.
Then under paragraph (c) there is the right to convey the waters of the Ghost river into lake Minnewanka through a canal extending from the park boundary to lake Minnewanka. The diversion of the water of the Ghost river is wholly a matter for the Alberta government. If that government says, "No, we will not permit diversion of water from the Ghost river," then of course the water from the Ghost river does not go into Minnewanka. It was necessary for us to give the company power to take water into the park from outside, into lake Minnewanka within the park. In doing so, it has to build a canal in order that the water may come from the Ghost river into lake Minnewanka for storage purposes. Again I submit there is nothing extraordinary in that paragraph.
Paragraph (d) conveys the right to construct transmission lines, with the necessary rights-of-way connecting the proposed power station with the existing transmission system. Quite obviously, if the company were going to develop power, it would require transmission lines to convey that power from the point of development to the point of use.

We have heard in the house during this session, from those who represent ag>
'cultural communities or communities which tre composed of industrial and agricultural see i ons, a great deal about wheat, coarse grains and the like. While at this late date one is possibly open to censure for discussing a matter which has not already been discussed, let alone questions which have been, I propose to speak on a matter which is of concern not only to my own constituency but to the whole area known as the southwestern Ontario peninsula, and better known, having in mind the matter which I wish to discuss, as the corn belt of Canada.
The counties vitally interested in this matter in southwestern Ontario are those of Essex- my own county-Kent, Lambton, Elgin and West Middlesex. Eighty-five per cent of the corn production of Canada is in that area, and the counties of Essex and Kent are responsible for 65 per cent of the total com production of this country. It is, of course, grown as a cash crop and is a vital factor in the income of the agricultural community in that area.
The recent agricultural policy of the government has affected that group and the ensuing farmers' income considerably. I do not propose to attack that policy but simply to indicate the effect which it has had upon this section of the agricultural community and to urge that a proposal which I brought before the house two or three sessions ago should be considered more fully and completely than it has been.

There is a similarity between agriculture as it is carried on in western Canada and in these counties, in contrast with the rest of Ontario, when one considers that the cash crops of these two latter find markets in central and eastern Ontario and not solely within the section where the corn crop itself is grown. The difference between agriculture in the counties in southwestern Ontario that I have mentioned and the rest of Ontario is illustrated by an analysis of the statistics of western feed grain shipped into Ontario recently from Fort William and Port Arthur under a freight subsidy plan jointly engaged in by the provincial and the federal governments. Under this plan, 1,900 carloads of feed grain were shipped into Ontario. The freight subsidy amounted to $338,000. Not a single car of this grain came into my own county of Essex or into the county of Lambton. Kent had four care, and the county of Elgin, two. Therefore only six cars out of 1,900 under this scheme were shipped into the corn-belt area, and the reason is that we are a surplus grain area in contrast with the rest of Ontario. The fact is, however, that the $330,000 paid by both governments, provincial and federal, was of no direct monetary value to the farmers in this area. Moreover, the com growers, being in possession of several million bushels of corn had to compete with western grains, and consequently their product was made cheaper on account of the favourable position in which western coarse grains found themselves as a result of the subsidy plan. This had a great effect on the price of com.
On December 16, 1940, the Minister of Agriculture announced that the government was considering a subsidy plan. Immediately the price of corn was depressed. The minister will recall that I then pointed out to him by telegram and in person the difficulty that would arise from a scheme which, although it is true it had been asked for by the province of Ontario, had not been considered in its full aspects and was bound to be disturbing to the farmers in the whole area of southwestern Ontario. The policy became effective in February, 1941, and the price of corn had fallen to ten cents. The committee will realize that a price of ten cents, having in mind that the tariff on corn is only ten cents, and having in mind also the difficulties which farmers in that part of the country must face in common with farmers in other parts of Canada, was a serious matter; so much so that the largest agency buying com in western Ontario announced on February 8, 1941, that, owing to the subsidy being granted by the government on feed grains from western Canada, prices for Ontario corn and other

Supply-Agriculture
grains were temporarily withdrawn. Not only that, but many of the farmers who sold during the first three months of this year lost ten cents a bushel as a direct result of the feed grain subsidy scheme and were put in a definitely discriminatory position.
I am not unaware of the difficulty of the Minister of Agriculture, and I will not go so far as to say that this freight subsidy plan, having in mind the demands of eastern agriculture, cannot possibly provoke a justifiable argument. What I am saying, however, is this, that if the scheme has the effect of embarrassing one section of the community, the onus is surely on the administration to consider ways and means of mitigating that. Before coming to what I have specifically in mind, I should point out that the recent plan of the administration to increase production of coarse grains in western Canada by paying subsidies for land taken out of wheat production will also be a detriment to the com growers of southwestern Ontario by reason of the added competition which these coarse grains will provide in the feed markets of eastern Ontario.
In March, 1938, I introduced in this house a resolution which was fully debated on all sides. The preamble indicated that there was a corn belt in Canada, that there was an area which produced at one time the entire corn consumptive needs of the country, and that every encouragement should be given to that area. The fact is that to-day we grow about
9.000.	000 bushels of corn and consume about
15.000.	000 bushels, and consequently we are compelled to import, mainly now from south Africa and the Argentine. The supplying of these importations under a definite policy on the part of the government, and greater encouragement to agriculture in that area, would bring about an increased acreage of corn production with subsequent benefit to the farmers from a financial point of view.
Having pointed out the problem generally in the preamble to that resolution, I urged upon the government two matters, and I urge them again. The first is that the government, in view of what I have just stated, should consider the necessity for improved marketing facilities and, second, the need for providing adequate storage, drying, government grading and inspection facilities in order that the quality of corn may be improved and the production increased. That resolution was adopted by the government of the day. The then Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking in this house in the face of opposition from some quarters, accepted it; and his acceptance, to me, could only mean that he
fully approved. Not having made any reservations, he could only have been assumed to concur in what the resolution sought to indicate. I regret to say, however, that while some interest has been displayed in this problem, no answer commensurate with what would seem to have been undertaken by the then Minister of Trade and Commerce has followed.
What did happen was that a member of the board of grain commissioners for the first time officially visited western Ontario, although western Ontario, from an agricultural point of view, is the most thickly populated area in Canada. As a result of the visit of this member of the board, Mr. Hamilton, it was decided to put in motion the operations of the wheat board. Consequently, with the setting up of this wheat board office went compulsory grading and inspection of wheat. Unfortunately, that compulsory feature was not applied to corn; and the figures, laborious as they may seem, nevertheless, even in the summarized form in which I propose to submit them, will indicate that if we could apply to agriculture, particularly to corn in southwestern Ontario, the same marketing principles that we have established with reference to wheat in western Canada, we would find occasion for considerable improvement.

This indicates clearly that where an attempt at inspection was made for the first time on a voluntary basis to try to assist in the marketing of this important commodity to the farmers of southwestern Ontario, the claim made by those who supported my resolution was more than justified. These figures show that the quantity of corn inspected during the last of the three crop years was nearly eight times the quantity of two years before and about 70 per cent greater than the quantity one year before.
Hon. members may ask, "Why this insistence on inspection?" The fact is that the com grown in that area has very often a moisture content of over 20 per cent. It should not be over 13 per cent in order to compete satisfactorily with corn grown in the Argentine, south Africa and even that which before the wTar was imported from the United States under a tariff of 10 per cent. Obviously the cornstarch people are not disposed to buy this product unless it is in a satisfactory state, and there is a great industrial market for it. I have urged the setting up of drying facilities to remove the excess moisture, and the establishment by the government of compulsory grading and inspection by government inspectors, so that, just as with regard to western wheat the trade throughout the world knows its quality by the official certificate attached, the farmers of southwestern Ontario might be placed in the same favourable position of being able, under the system I propose, to have their commodity, once it has been properly certified, stand on its merits as does western wheat.
After Mr. Hamilton visited southwestern Ontario, he made a report, which is available to anyone who wishes to see it. It was made

Supply-Agriculture
to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, not the present minister who I am glad to see in his seat to-day, following my discussion I hope with great diligence and proper profit to himself. This report states:
Before investigating the matter on the ground

I presume meaning western Ontario.
*-I proceeded to Ottawa and interviewed the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It was decided that the investigation should be limited to the grading of corn; that the question of providing storage and drying facilities did not come under the board of grain commissioners.
That statement indicates that the question has not been approached in the comprehensive way in which it should be approached, because there have been subsequent reports made by the officials of the government, the last being by the agricultural supplies board together with a private survey that has been made, and reported in a valuable compilation entitled "A Survey of Canadian Research on the Utilization of Farm Products" issued by the national chemurgic committee of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. At page 12 of that report will be found substantiation of what I have argued before in this house and of my argument now, and of what government reports themselves indicate to be the only solution of this problem. I wish to quote one or two excerpts, removed perhaps from their context, but nevertheless not unfairly. Under the head of "corn starch" the report states:
This is the principal starch produced in this country and is made almost exclusively from imported corn, which at the present time is mainly of South African origin.
Then it goes on to say:
Starch factories have little fault to find with the quality of Ontario corn except that it is generally very high in moisture when offered. . . .
And here is a significant statement:
If particular emphasis was being placed on what is now imported that we could produce ourselves, it would be difficult to justify the importation of starch or any of its products, or of corn for their manufacture. The requirements of starch and cereal manufacturers could be largely met by Canadian corn, even if it may not be quite as satisfactory as corn grown in more torrid zones, provided an adequate marketing scheme could be worked out. Manufacturers claim that, in the past, they have experienced great difficulty in getting orders filled on the domestic market. Shipping facilities have been poor, all of the corn having to be moved by rail since no elevator is available on the St. Clair river or on the lake front.
There, succinctly stated, is the answer. There is no quarrel with the commodity itself; the difficulty is with regard to the moisture content and particularly the inability of the trade to
get the corn in large quantities on account of the absence of storage facilities and also because the trade has not faith in the commodity grown here since it does not bear the certification of a government-inspected and government-created scheme.
Another aspect of the matter was brought to my attention, and to the attention of others in western Ontario, after the present war began. It was pointed out that since we grew only half the com consumed in Canada, and since the farmers were not disposed to increase their acreage by reason of the difficulties I have enumerated, in the absence of a proper marketing scheme on the part of the government we were compelled to import almost half our total requirements.
This importation of com from south Africa, the United States, and particularly the Argentine, was brought to the attention of the agricultural supplies board headed by Doctor E. S. Archibald, who has made an analysis of this problem, which analysis is, I presume, available to the Minister of Agriculture and to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Doctor Archibald points out that approximately four million bushels of imported corn is now being used for industrial purposes, and this at a time when we have set up embargoes against the importation of many other commodities. He goes on to say that a considerable quantity of the imported corn used for feed also can be classed as used for industrial purposes, since it is used by manufacturers of mixed feed for poultry, hogs and other live stock. In order that industries such as those mentioned can be properly served, Doctor Archibald points out that the four requirements which I have discussed in another way must be fulfilled. Those requirements are: continuity of supply, the necessity of having the corn properly dried, grading and inspection, and facilities for shipping by either water or rail.
I am not quarrelling with what the administration has done under the freight subsidy plan in respect of coarse grains. Nor do I quarrel with its policy with regard to the reduction of wheat acreage. I do point out, however, the unfair position in which the Ontario farmer is placed. If this government is sincere in trying to meet this problem, surely we can no longer delay in providing suitable facilities for storing this corn in bulk, having it properly inspected and graded on a compulsory basis in order to satisfy the demands of the trade, and assisting in setting up those agencies by which the corn can be satisfactorily dried. Doctor Archibald concludes his report by suggesting a solution, which Mr. Hamilton was not permitted to do under the terms of his reference. Doctor Archibald says:
Supply-Agriculture

Before it (Ontario corn) could be used on a large scale for industrial purposes, it is probable that facilities for storing and drying would have to be made available.
I have given this matter a good deal of study and attention. There have been conferences galore with departmental officials. There has been a disposition to consider that the farmers in those areas where there is a large measure of industrialization are thereby provided with a market not open to their fellow farmers in the rest of the country, at least during the war. While I do not deny that, the fact is that in southwestern Ontario agricultural costs are higher, and upon close analysis the benefit of heavy industrialization is not as great as it may seem. I have attended the meetings of this house assiduously, day after day; I do not think anyone will accuse me of shirking my responsibility in that regard. I have followed the arguments advanced by hon. members who come from western Canada, and I know something of western Canada myself, having visited that section of the country frequently. In comparing the lot of the farmer whom I represent, or of the farmers throughout the so-called rich area of southwestern Ontario, I doubt very much if the difference in the standard of living as between the farmer of the east and the farmer of the west would be as great over the long pull as many imagine.
The government has met the wheat problem, at least so far as an approach to it is concerned; the government has met the problem of the dairy farmer, but it has not met the problem of that area in which most of the Ontario wheat and 85 per cent of the corn of this country are grown. If we go on in the haphazard way that has been followed in the past there will be only one thing for the farmers in that area to do, namely, go out of corn production. That would mean heavier importations. That would mean that the starch companies, instead of buying their corn from us, would continue to buy it from the United States, and this at a time when we are at war and when we are concerned with the conservation of exchange. Surely we cannot postpone dealing with this problem any longer. If the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce do me the honour of replying, I hope the Minister of Agriculture will not say that this is not his problem. Following that, I certainly hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce will not say that it is not his problem either, because that is the way in which this matter has been shifted round. This is a marketing problem. Surely the policy to be laid down is a matter for the Minister of Agriculture. The setting up of a storage plant under private or public auspices, 
following the suggestions that have been advanced, may be a matter for the Department of Trade and Commerce or perhaps for the Department of Transport. Nevertheless this is a problem which the government cannot shirk any longer. We wish to improve the position of the farmers in that area so far as corn is concerned; and I am sure every hon. member from western Ontario will agree that the time has come when, first, we must put our commodity in exactly the same position with regard to moisture as corn coming from other countries; and, second, that having done this, we must set up a satisfactory marketing scheme which will take account of the matters of compulsory grading and inspection that I have indicated.
I have just one further word. Latterly the province of Ontario and the federal government have been engaged in a survey of this matter. Since I hav.e been a member of this house, there have been no less than six surveys of this whole problem. One would be almost inclined to think that the resistance to the sort of barrage I am putting up to-day is a survey. However, perhaps this time something is contemplated, because an effort has been made on behalf of the farmers of that area to institute a marketing scheme on a compulsory basis. The dominion government argued that it did not have the constitutional authority to deal with that matter, but now I understand that the two governments are dealing with the problem or at least propose to deal with it after the survey has been made. I am not a farmer; I simply represent a district in which this problem is acute, but I do urge that we should have a definite policy so that year after year we shall not be dealing with this matter in a haphazard, unscientific manner which indicates a clear lack of planning. There is a real marketing problem here. Officers of the crown have supported the contentions I am making, and all that remains now is for the government to carry out the recommendations that have been made. I am sure that if this is done and a compulsory scheme instituted, with proper drying and storage facilities provided, the result will be a great improvement in this branch of agriculture. I earnestly urge that the Department of Agriculture, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce take hold of this problem in a way that will call forth our everlasting gratitude.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Just before the dinner recess the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) was reviewing the position in relation to corn, particularly that obtaining in the southwestern part of Ontario where the greater volume of corn is produced. The figures for Ontario for 1939 show a production of a little over 8,000,000 bushels, and in 1940, almost
7.000.	000 bushels. Over a period of six years there has been an average production of
9.000.	000 bushels. There is very little information with regard to the production in other parts of Canada prior to 1939. Manitoba had a production of 1,600,000 bushels in 1940. In previous years prices have been running from 55 cents up to 65 cents for Ontario producers. I think on May 20 of this year the price was
75 cents a bushel at the farm in Ontario, with trucking to elevator costing approximately two cents a bushel, making the price at the elevator 77 cents a bushel. The day before this memorandum was made up, which was within the last few days, the United States price was 71 cents a bushel for No. 1 corn at Chicago. Those are some of the facts with regard to the situation.
The hon. member for Essex East referred to the fact that corn produced in Canada, particularly that produced in the southwestern part of Ontario, has a fairly high moisture content. On account of this high moisture content and the fact that we have no proper facilities for drying com, the product sometimes arrives in poor shape for feeding purposes in Ontario or other parts of eastern Canada. Different departments of government in recent years have been faced with the problem of providing driers at some particular points or an elevator or elevators with driers attached, in order that the corn may be handled more efficiently and in better condition. The report which was read before the dinner recess was prepared by the chambers of commerce, and it states that Canadian corn is suitable for commercial as well as feeding purposes, the main difficulty being that which was outlined to the committee by the hon. member for Essex East, namely, the high moisture content.
As was stated, consideration has been given to this problem on a number of occasions. I think that each time those who have investigated the matter have agreed on the methods which ought to be followed in order to handle the corn properly. Most of those who have investigated and dealt with the matter from the point of view of providing suitable feed for live stock have maintained that the cheapest way to dry this corn is in cribs upon the farms. It was stated that it takes from two to four months to dry com, depending upon its condition and the time of year in which it is being dried. In order, however, to provide for shipments in the early months of the shipping season, it is necessary to have some artificial means of drying, if the corn is to arrive in good condition. So far as the preparation of com for commercial purposes is concerned, it seems that it is essential that artificial driers should be established at one or more points.
The question is one which brings up the old difficulty that arises quite often in connection with different problems associated with agriculture and other industries in Canada, namely, that of provincial responsibility as against federal responsibility. Something was . said about that by the hon. member for Essex East, and at this time I would only say that
Supply-Agriculture

we would not care to carry that argument further than to say that where the greater part of a product is produced in the same province in which it is consumed, we would be desirous of at least having the advice and consent of the provincial authorities in connection with anything that we might undertake to do. We would prefer to have representations made to us from the provincial governments to the effect that they desire to have something done to putting pressure on provincial governments in connection with products of that kind. I think that inquiries which are being made as between the provincial and the federal government may result in something being done which will be helpful.
In connection with the construction of an elevator, it was stated by the hon. member for Essex East that we had been more or less passing the buck between departments in years gone by. He suggested that the Department of Agriculture was inclined to say that this was the responsibility of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and he now sug-gets that the opinion is passed on that it is really the responsibility of the Department of Transport. I have made some inquiries into the matter, and I am convinced that the responsibility in so far as the construction of elevators east of Fort William is concerned, belongs to the Department of Transport. At the same time I am not going to shirk the responsibility of dealing with the matter as an agricultural problem. I am quite prepared to say to the hon. member that the department is quite anxious to give consideration to any representations that may be made to us or that have been made to us from the counties concerned, namely, the four or five counties in the southwestern part of Ontario. I would only suggest that we shall consider them subject to discussions which we may have with the provincial government.
I admit at once that some improved shipping facilities are necessary. I admit that some method of drying grain is essential to the proper handling of com. I admit also that the government should take an interest in both these problems and try to find a solution of the problem confronting the people in that section of the province, more particularly in this period when we are interested in the production of corn, not only for commercial purposes but as a feed, and a good feed, especially in connection with the production of hogs which is so necessary at the present time. I think this is all that I can say at the moment until the matter has been fully discussed with the members of the governments concerned and with the government itself.
(Mr. Gardiner.)

I did not plan on pursuing the interesting argument advanced by the hon. member for Essex East, but in passing I should like to say that the apparent consideration which he has given to this subject and the interesting maimer in which he has presented it should satisfy all hon. members that it is not necessary to be a farmer from one of the back concessions of Ontario in order to be able to discuss important agricultural problems. At eleven o'clock last night I was discussing the stamp plan in the United States, and the Minister of Agriculture mentioned that the Canadian government had distributed large quantities of butter, cheese, fish and other commodities. I am aware that the government have done a good deal in this field, but I contend that they have not gone nearly far enough, nor have they undertaken the problem in the systematic way which characterizes the stamp plan in the United States. On a former occasion I made reference to a book prepared by the Canadian Medical association, "Food1 for Health". A paragraph I did not quote before is found on the front page:
By eating the proper kind and amount of food, you and your family are protecting yourselves against the diseases which go along with war and which spread in the period immediately following. In addition, good health enables wage-earners to stay on the job. Working time lost through sickness usually means a smaller pay envelope. We have a war to win. We must be fit for -whatever task is required of us. Every housewife can do her bit-and help others do theirs by keeping her family's health at a high level.
On the fifth page, in heavy print:
The Canadian farmer produces all the foods necessary for good health. Canadian grown vegetables such as tomatoes, turnips, cabbage, and fruits in season (apples, berries, cherries, plums, peaches, pears) can replace the more expensive imported fruits.
I am sure that hon. members were ashamed last night to hear what I read from a newspaper, to the effect that literally thousands of boxes of apples in British Columbia had been dumped. Other surplus foods are going to waste in Canada, and yet in this dominion there are people who are not getting enough to satisfy a decent standard of living. I am not able to say what number of people in this country are not getting enough to eat, but the last report submitted by the Department of Labour in connection with the Unemployment and Agricultural Assistance Act sets forth, on page 34, that in March, 1941, there were in Canada 325,000 individuals on direct relief. If the people on direct relief in other parts of this country are in the same position as those on direct relief in my con-

Supply-Agriculture
stituency, there are in this dominion a great many people who are not getting enough to eat.
I am not going to discuss all the foods which are available in Canada, but I shall refer briefly to one important food, namely, wheat or flour. Last evening I made reference to a school attendance officer in my constituency who reported that three families in his district are unable to send their children to school because they do not have flour in the house; and the information I have from my constituency is that notices have gone out to people on relief that there will be no more relief. I feel confident that the department at Regina will reconsider this decision, and that cases where it is impossible for them to manage without assistance will receive further aid. In the meantime, I feel sure, a great many families found themselves at the end of last month with no money, no credit at the store, and no way of securing flour except by imposing upon the good graces of the storekeeper.
In another vote the minister has asked us for $35,000,000 for the purpose of not growing wheat. Surely his department should be able, in conjunction with the Department of Trade and Commerce, to find means of providing that some of the surplus wheat in Canada is made available under a plan similar to the stamp plan in the United States, so that every householder in the nation shall have all the flour necessary to supply bread to his table three times a day. The minister should explain, when he is asking this parliament for $1,735,590.64 in connection with his marketing services, why he is not in a position to find ways and means of providing that all the wheat necessary shall be available to make bread for hungry children in this country.
The article in the pamphlet to which I have referred, stressing the importance of guarding the health of Canada, cannot be overemphasized. The minister would do well to give careful consideration to the carrying out of the principles of some plan like the stamp plan, or evolve a plan of his own, so that not a single family in this dominion will be denied the right to all the wheat products which they can possibly use.

About a week or ten days ago, I believe, the hon. member for Fraser Valley made inquiry of the Prime Minister when the house would be prorogued or adjourned. Of course, the Prime Minister could not very well answer that question, because, while it is a well-known fact that the party in power summons parliament and sets the date when it will be opened, the opposition always decides when it will be prorogued or adjourned.
Not this time.

That opposition may come from the official opposition or from hon. members of the various opposition groups, but that is the quarter where the opposition must come from, or the item would pass. Therefore the logic of the situation is, probably, why talk about an item concerning something which is already in force or in operation? You cannot change it anyway.
In order to clarify my position, may I recall to hon. members that, just before the Easter recess, when we were passing legislation embodying the wheat policy for the west, I endeavoured to make a few remarks around six o'clock and I was ruled out of order, but I was assured that I would have an opportunity to make those observations at a later date. It makes quite a difference whether a policy which is being discussed is or is not actually in effect. In any event, I wish to make a few casual remarks.
The Minister of Agriculture inserted in the estimates an item which has to do with his wheat policy. May I say that if the minister believed he had a policy which would be acceptable to all the agricultural interests from British Columbia to Prince Edward Island, he must now be the most disillusioned man in the house. As a matter of fact, the thing is impossible, and I believe that the minister realizes it.
I have followed since 1938 the policy of the Minister of Agriculture with regard to wheat legislation, and I believe that any one who has done so cannot but admit that from that time up to the present he has certainly been a "sugar-daddy" to western Canada. If the people in the west are not satisfied with his wheat legislation, I do not believe it is possible to satisfy them.
A good many objections were raised by hon. members, some from western Canada, to the effect that his policy was one of regimentation, that the farmers were told they had to do this and they had to do that. As an actual fact, that was not the situation; there was nothing compulsory about the matter, as was evidenced by the statement of the hon. member for Moose Jaw that he intended to do just as he had always done-go on and grow wheat. I have, however, no doubt that the Minister of Agriculture wanted to make and did make a policy so attractive to western agriculturists in general that they would accept it. In my opinion he made a very good job of it. For instance, he offered $4 an acre for summer-fallow, up to a certain percentage anyway, which was taken out of wheat
Supply-Agriculture

cultivation. I would say that $4 an acre is very attractive. I well remember that the hon. member who occupies the seat beside me-he is not here to-night-has some property in the west. I was witness to his signature on some leases which he was sending out west, and the sum he was paying for land summer-fallowing was $2.50 an acre. He mentioned that he had been getting the same work done in previous years for $2 an acre. I well remember, too, that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who is, I believe he will admit, a big wheat farmer, claimed that he was getting summer-fallowing done at $1.50 an acre, and that he could have hundreds and perhaps thousands of acres summer-fallowed at that price. The policy adopted by the Minister of Agriculture must have been quite attractive. I remember, when we were discussing certain property in the vicinity of an experimental farm at Rosthern, the hon. member for Wood Mountain, I believe, said that land there could be bought for as low as ten dollars an acre. Therefore, if one summer-fallowed land there for two and a half years, he would have the land for nothing anyway.
I agree with the hon. member for Essex East. I am not going to belabour this question, because he went into it fully, and I am in accord with what he said. Coarse grains were quite a problem, and the Minister of Agriculture declared that in his opinion it would not influence or affect the eastern farmer, but he said it so often that I rather think he believed it himself. I am quite satisfied that it is discriminating against the coarse-grain growers of the east. Barley is a good substitute for corn; and if you bonus it in the west and pay the freight on it to the east, it is decidedly in competition with corn produced in southwestern Ontario. I do not think the policy is quite fair to the corn growers of the country.
When the question was brought up before, I said that we grew all the grain we required, even last year under abnormal conditions. That is not quite true, although the southwestern counties did not import any western grain. I wish to make it quite clear that I am not opposed to western agriculture. I should like to see the western farmers get as much as they can; I should like to see them get a dollar a bushel for their wheat. But what I did object to, and what I object to now under that policy, is that eastern agriculture cannot afford to pay for a bonusing policy for the west. That is what I objected to, and I still object to it.
I was also opposed, and naturally so, to the way in which the measure was brought

down. The government used their powers under the War Measures Act to frame a policy and to deal with the matter in supply where there was no opportunity to move amendments or to change the regulations. The whole question should have been discussed in the committee on agriculture before it was brought into the house, and, if necessary, there should have been appropriate amendments which would have made the legislation workable and agreeable to all parts of the country.
I agree that on the whole agriculture has been getting a rather better deal of late; things are looking up a little. We must admit, however, tliat agricultural prices should be placed on a parity with prices of other commodities if we are ever to be on a sound economic basis in Canada. No party has, however, offered any policy or solution or panacea for this problem. They all say that something should be done, but they do not come forward with a concrete plan to put agriculture on a sound economic basis. The old law of supply and demand no longer operates; at least it does not function to the extent that it did before. That is true not only now but of the pre-war period. We must look for some solution if we are ever to put agriculture on a sound basis. When the war is over and we get back to a sound trading policy, the situation will probably clear up; but I have my doubts, because throughout the world we find no common standard of living, no common standard of wages, no common standard of money. I could mention several instances. I could discuss at some length the question of beet sugar. Cane sugar can be bought cheaper than beet sugar because the labour employed in harvesting the cane receives forty cents a day; but one cannot procure labour in our fields at less than $2.50 or $3 a day. The same is true of other commodities, and we are exporting only a small proportion of our agricultural products. There is no market for butter outside the dominion, and we have no large exports with the possible exception of wheat. We should, therefore, devise some plan of controlling prices and, to some extent, production. If the government could bring in some sort of national marketing act and work out a system of our own to place agriculture on a sound and safe economic basis, it would be a great boon to the farmers.

I wish to commend the argument put forward by the hon. member for Essex East with regard to the growing of corn in Canada to supply our corn starch manufacturing plants. I have had some experience with com starch, and I believe

Supply-Agriculture
there are two plants in Ontario, one at Cardinal and the other at Port Credit. Those plants have large storage facilities, and all that would be necessary would :be to install drying apparatus. The corn could be taken from the fields and dried in those plants. At present they import com in the fall from south Africa and south America, bringing it -here before navigation closes.
And the United States.

There must be large storage facilities at those plants. Manitoba can grow good corn. Why, then, send out foreign exchange for com at the present time? Most of it is coming from the United States to-day to supply the factories, and there is a large export demand for com starch. The United States is shipping millions of tons of com starch to Europe and all the other countries of the world.

I am not going to make a speech to-night. I was told that I was on the wrong item when I tried to discuss certain questions before, but I believe I am in order to-night. I wish to make one correction. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent made reference to western Canada. Let me inform the committee that, geographically speaking, British Columbia is in the west, although apparently the committee does not know this. We do not grow wheat, but we are in the west nevertheless.
Although I do not agree that the minister is a "sugar-daddy" to anybody-knowing his record in the past, I do not think he would not be a "sugar-daddy" according to my definition of that term-I am particularly interested in what will happen to eggs and poultry. Last night, it seems, I was in the wrong section, but I should like to have some explanation from the minister. I was informed that he did not have the right bodyguard or officials round him to give him the information on marketing. May I ask him what is to happen to that other war casualty in my riding, the small fruit grower. In British Columbia we depend upon our export surplus.
Unfortunately, owing to the war and shipping conditions, we have not been able to dispose of our extra berries, our processed berries, to Great Britain. I give the minister full credit that last year he was able to dispose of them, but I should like to know what provision is being made this year. The growers in my constituency must know now, because they are now starting to can those berries, probably with such a fine climate as British Columbia has, they are already canned, and we must know where we are going to dispose of
them. Before this session closes-and I do not wish to have to talk for three days-I think we should know whether we are or are not going to get the same treatment for eggs as is given for butter, honey, maple sugar, lobster, apples and wheat. I repeat that word "wheat." It is a commodity grown in a couple of the provinces. We should like to know if we are going to get a minimum guaranteed price that will at least return the cost of production. Under this item of marketing services administration, I think the minister should be in a position, in view of his statement of last year, that the same treatment would be accorded to all producers in every part of Canada, to give us some assurance.

I should like
to add a word or two, not altogether along the same lines but along one vital line, namely, the matter of getting fruit through to the British isles. I have in my files three or four letters from those now overseas who find themselves unable to satisfy their requirements with regard to fruit and fruit juices. They ask for more apples from Canada, if necessary dried apples in order to save the freight, and they particularly ask whether it is possible to get apple juice. The condition which at present obtains is that companies such as Eaton's, Simpson's and other large department stores in Canada have arranged to pack for shipment overseas parcels of fruit juices such as tomato, apple and some orange juice which their friends here send to the boys overseas. One of my constituents writes me that there is a shortage over there of vitamins;
I think it is vitamin C. It seems uneconomical for interested people in Canada to have to mail cans of apple juice overseas, the cost of mailing being four or five or six times the cost of the product itself. Yet people do so in order to satisfy the needs of their loved ones who are serving in the forces overseas. What I had in mind is that this marketing service * might take hold of this matter in a rather big way and send overseas our tomato juice which contains this required vitamin, and our apple juice, dried apples and fruits of all kinds. So much for the local situation mentioned by the hon. member for Fraser Valley.
Passing now to the world situation, we find that our markets on the European continent are very much disrupted. We have been taught by the exponents of the policy of the Liberal party that overseas trade, and more particularly trade with Europe, is the lifeblood of this country. That trade has been demoralized by the present conflict. I am wondering what policy the Minister of Agriculture has in mind to improve Canada's position in view of our being cut off from that market, the result being, as we all know
Supply-Agriculture

that in Canada we have a surplus of agricultural products. That surplus causes prices of these products to fall to a low level. Subsidize as much as you will; assist as much as you will by bonuses and subsidies of the kind that have been enunciated here, namely, $4 per acre if you make the ground black and in the way of becoming a desert again, or $2 per acre if you put it into coarse grain.
The spending of these odd millions, $35,000,000 in that instance, will not help the situation in the long run. In fact I am greatly concerned about the position we are getting into through these grants and allowances for having land black in July. I am concerned about the state it will be in by July of next year. It may be a desert. If it is, then we shall not be in a position to produce, even though, on account of the lack of a market for that extra 10 or 15 or 20 per cent in Europe, we have at present a depressed level of agricultural prices. Let us not be too much concerned about that, even though in Europe they have a false or pseudo-prosperity. Analyse that situation, due to the fact that a bushel of wheat in Germany to-day may buy $2 worth of goods and services, whereas in Canada a bushel of wheat will buy only fifty cents worth; in the matter of a decade that will prove only a false or pseudo-prosperity. On account of that false prosperity, goods and services are coming back to the producers of wheat, bacon and other consumable commodities to an amount out of proportion to what those goods and sendees are really worth.
In our land of prosperity and abundance the reverse obtains. Therefore I say to my hon. friends who concern themselves about the low price of agricultural and other products and materials which by nature we are able to produce, that this condition is probably just temporary and the world equation will soon balance itself. The world equation may balance itself, and even though the present situation is difficult; even though the economic pressure we have exerted against the totalitarian states has not worked to the extent that we had hoped, the day will come when they will want our goods. Therefore I say to the Canadian producer of primary commodities, "Stay with us in farm production and in the long run we shall win through." That prosperity wjiich obtains in the totalitarian countries, due to a shortage of the goods they would like to consume, in the final analysis will bring about their defeat. When the men rescued from the Bismarck had their first meal on board a British ship they were amazed when they were served a full-course dinner. They were not accustomed to a full stomach on which to work. That is the very thing that will pull us through. Therefore I say to the

minister, and to all those who are looking to him to save agriculture in Canada to-day, that they should have patience, because in the long run we in Canada, together with the other members of the British commonwealth that have large supplies of these commodities, will get these commodities through to Britain.
That is the job of the minister; he must see that Britain gets these goods. We are all glad and willing to help in any way possible that this may be done, whether it is eggs from British Columbia, wheat from the prairie provinces, fruit from the land of Evangeline, or pork from the eight million hogs throughout Canada; let us get these products through to Britain. It is said that armies travel on their stomachs. Let us make sure that the Englishmen, the Canadians and all those fighting in our behalf have full stomachs on which to fight, even though prices are low here. The people of the totalitarian states are almost starving for those commodities of which we have an abundance; and when this conflict is over-pray God that may be fairly soon-they will want those products and we shall be able to reestablish our channels of trade. Then, once more Canada will return to her place as one of the greatest exporters of primary products. Consequently I hope the minister will tell us what the marketing service has in mind with regard to securing those commodities of which the United Kingdom is short, and, beyond that, supplying an abundance of all commodities, without regard to cost, so that the armed forces of the United Kingdom may give a good account of themselves and, at the same time, we may escape the difficult situation in which we find ourselves to-day.
Might I have an answer to my question? I have to attend a committee meeting, and I do not wish to have to listen to all this oratory.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The hon. member for Fraser Valley has asked for information with regard to the possibility of marketing certain fruits which have to be disposed of in British Columbia each fall. Last year we made an arrangement with Great Britain whereby they agreed to take delivery of 1,700 tons of the type of berry products in which the hon. member is interested. We found that we were able to deliver only 1,300 tons, for the reason that this was all we were able to obtain at that time by way of surplus. This year the marketing branch of the department is negotiating with the same authorities in Britain for an arrangement under which they will take somewhere between 1,700 and 2,500 tons.

Supply-Agriculture
The minister is referring to processed fruit, is he?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes, processed berries. The negotiations have not been completed, but we expect that an arrangement similar to that of last year will be arrived at, and we hope it will take care of any surplus that may be available this fall.
With regard to eggs, we have had some little difficulty until very recently. During last month, I understand that we completed the shipment of 180,000 cases of fresh eggs to Britain, and we are making arrangements to deliver more than 230,000 cases this fall; we are storing them now for delivery at that time. I quite appreciate that this is a very small proportion of the eggs produced in Canada, but I think I am correct in saying that we were shipping only a very small proportion of our eggs to Britain before the war. Then, again, it is just possible that we have a greater production at the present time on account of a general stepping up of production of all farm products throughout the country, and it may be necessary for us to dispose of a larger quantity than we have in mind at the present time. In any event, negotiations are going forward looking to the disposal of that surplus.
With reference to the other questions raised by the hon. member for Danforth, I do not think the situation is exactly as his remarks might lead one to believe. We are disposing of more farm products of every kind1-
Would the minister address himself to apple juice and tomato juice?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I will come to those. We are disposing of more of the stable farm products generally exported from Canada, with the exception of wheat, than was the situation before the war.
We quite agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have had some difficulty with regard to apples. Before the war we exported to Britain fifty per cent of the apples grown in Canada, while in the Annapolis valley of Nova Scotia the export figure reached approximately 80 per cent. During the first fall of the war, at some inconvenience to herself Britain did take a certain proportion of our fresh apples from the maritime provinces and British Columbia, but during the second year they did not desire to take delivery of fresh apples. One reason for that was that apples are bulky in relation to their food value and take considerable shipping space which is of greater importance to Britain at the present time in connection with other foods.
I asked particularly about dried apples.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am coming to those. In the first fall of the war not only did we deliver a certain percentage of our apples to Great Britain; the government itself took over the remainder of the apples, which were canned or dehydrated. I think we still have some of those apples which were grown in 1939, and canned in the winter of 1939-40. We have given away some of them. We have sold some of them. We gaT_e some to some people who told us afterwards that they would just as soon we had not shipped them.
Nova Scotia apples?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
They were dehydrated apples. That statement was made, not because the apples were not good enough, but because they took up shipping space at a time when other foods of greater importance had not enough shipping space. Under those conditions, of course we are not pressing our apple crop upon the British people.
I may say that when I was in England last fall I did discover some apples in a market in Liverpool. I made some inquiries as to how they got there, knowing that we were not shipping any apples from Canada. I did not understand how apples might have been received from some other countries. When I made inquiries I found out that the apples were some Which had been taken off a captured boat, and were being disposed of simply because they had been landed in Great Britain.
Distress apples.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I state this in order to indicate that the British people are not taking apples at the present time in anything like the quantities they were taken before. They are not taking fresh apples at all, so far as I know and, from what I can learn, they are not anxious to receive even dehydrated apples, and certainly not in the quantities we could supply. In other words, we have some difficulty in disposing of our apple crop. It is costing the government about $2,000,000 a year to take off the market apples which cannot be disposed of and which, had there been no war, would have been disposed of in Great Britain.
I believe that the same observations would apply to a greater or lesser degree to apple and other fruit juices. Perhaps it applies to a lesser degree on account of the fact that the juices may be canned and shipped in a form which is not as objectionable as fresh apples would be. At the present time, however, there is not any considerable demand; as a matter of fact, there is no demand at all for them.
Supply-Agriculture
Do I understand the minister to say that there is no demand for fruit juices?
