speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have no request for fruit juices up to the present time; but for tomato juice there is a demand.

With all due
deference to the minister, there is a great demand for orange, apple and tomato juices.
Who is making the speech?
The minister is, but I am correcting him.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I can only answer the questions I have been asked from the information we have in the department. If the hon. member for Danforth has other information, I should be very glad to have it.

There is a
shortage of apple and tomato juices.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is scarcely correct to imply that agriculture is not doing as well in the matter of volume shipped from this country, or in the matter of price received-
No such inference can be drawn from what I have said.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: -at the present time, as it did before the war. In other words, Great Britain is taking from Canada to-day very much greater quantities of pork products than we sold to all countries to which we delivered pork products before the war.
I agree.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: In other words, we are not shipping less; we are shipping very much more.
I agree with that. The minister has no right to draw the inference that I said anything different.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I believe I had better try to answer the inference-
There was no inference at all.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
-and have the information complete. My memory is that in the last complete year before the war we shipped about 160,000,000 pounds of Wiltshire sides to Great Britain. This year we shall ship
450,000,000 pounds, or almost three times as much. While the actual market price as it would prevail upon the market if nothing were done about it, other than to accept the terms of the agreement, is approximately the same as the market price in that earlier year, the government of Great Britain raised that price

a short time ago in order to assist in bringing the price up to the level of the United States price. That was done by increasing the price allowed us under the agreement from 80 shillings to 85 shillings. Since that time, the government of Canada has added an additional 75 cents per hundred pounds of Wiltshire sides, in order that Canada might do her part in increasing the price up to the level which has been produced in the United States market.
This has been done for a twofold purpose: first, for the purpose of giving the best return we can arrange at the present time. Whether it is satisfactory to agriculture all the way across Canada, I am not going to try to argue. It has, however, been for the purpose of securing the best price which we consider we could arrange. That price is a little bit higher now than was the price in the year of the first agreement. I think farmers across Canada have expressed themselves as being fairly well satisfied with the price * we obtained in the first year of the agreement. The price prevailing now is better.
That 75 cents is included?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes. It was a little better even before we added the 75 cents.
Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Would the hon. member permit me to finish my answer to his speech? The second purpose is to encourage the farmers to produce still more next year. The present position is that Great Britain is taking all the surplus pork products, and particularly Wiltshire sides, that we have available to ship to her. We are shipping it- all, in so far as bottoms can be secured. I believe she will be prepared to take all the Wiltshire sides we can produce, or that we are likely to produce-I shall .put it in that way-within the next twelve months.
We want the farmers to understand that the government of Canada, along with the government of Great Britain, is and will be prepared to see to it that in view of the circumstances a reasonable price is maintained, to the end that we may get the highest possible production.
That brings me to the reference made a few minutes ago to the policy which has been followed in connection with wheat. It has been suggested that we simply bonused the farmers to the extent of 14 an acre, in order to have them keep their land idle. That is not what we did. We asked the farmers to reduce their wheat acreage, and we gave our reasons for doing so. We said, "We have now

Supply-Agriculture
enough wheat in storage in Canada to supply all Great Britain's needs, all our own needs and all the needs of any other countries to which we have any reason to believe we shall be supplying wheat within the next two years." We have enough wheat in storage now to supply purchasers for two years. We said, further, "It is costing the government of Canada a certain amount of money to take delivery of that wheat, in order to make it possible for the people who grow it to live." The amount that we have been paying out is 70 cents a bushel Fort William for every bushel of wheat delivered. Then we would add to that about ten cents a bushel a year in storage and carrying charges for each year the wheat is going to be carried. If we carry it into the third year, having two years' supply already on hand, it will cost the government about one dollar a bushel to take delivery of that wheat and carry it until such time as there is a demand for it.
We have said to the people of western Canada; we have said to the people of all Canada that, on that basis, for every bushel of wheat that they keep out of production, that is, every bushel of wheat that they do not produce this year, they will be making available from the amount of money that the government of Canada has to raise one dollar to be expended during the next three years in prosecuting the war. It was on that basis that the pamphlets, which were quoted here last evening and which were referred to again to-day, were put out in western Canada. Those pamphlets were to the effect that to grow less wheat in 1941-not grow less wheat in 1942 or in 1943-would help in the prosecution of the war. I say that to reduce the bushelage by a million bushels which the government would have had to take delivery of will help in the prosecution of the war financially to the extent of one dollar a bushel for the three years; to the extent of $1,000,000 for every 1,000,000 bushels
It was upon that basis that we asked the farmers of western Canada to reduce their acreage this year. We said, "We are not coming to the people of western Canada at the present time and saying that you should not grow wheat; we are not coming to the people of western Canada and saying that at some future time you should not grow wheat; we are coming to them and we are saying two things, first, that there are certain products that ought to be produced this year in greater volume than you have been producing them before. We want more butter; we want more hogs; we want more cattle, and if we are going to be able to produce these products in Canada we must have more feed grain."
We said, "In addition to helping us out in financing the war by not asking the government to take delivery of the same amount of wheat this year that they have in the last two years, if you grow more coarse grains, either you will make it possible to produce these other products on the farms where you are growing the crops or by shipping them to some other part of Canada you will be making possible the production of these other products in other parts of Canada."
Up to date the reports indicate that the farmers of western Canada followed our advice in the matter, and advices up to the present indicate that they have reduced their acreage by close to 7,000,000 acres. That is, out of a total acreage of somewhere around 27,000,000 acres, they have cut off about 7,000,000 acres. Some of that land is being put into summer-fallow, and to the extent that they have reduced wheat acreage they will be paid $4 an acre for having done so. My hon. friend says that he fears a desert next year. I do not fear a desert as a result of summerfallowing in western Canada, but I would say there is a possibility that we may have more wheat next year because we summer-fallowed this year.

That would be
all right.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
This summer-fallowing
may amount to three or four million acres this year. The hon. member for Danforth says, "That w'ould be all right." I think it will be all right from the point of view of having a greater production next year. I am not one of those who think it is a good thing over a period of time to reduce the production of food. In the long fun I think it is probably a good thing to increase the production of food.	While it may be
necessary this year to cut down the production of wheat on account of the position in which we find ourselves in relation to the whole problem, in the long run I do not think any harm is going to come from having three or four million acres of land in a better condition to produce more grain next year, whether it be wheat if we want it, or whether it be more coarse grains in order that we may produce more of other products.
The remainder of the six, seven, or eight million acres, whatever it may turn out to be, which has been taken out of wheat will be put into coarse grains and grasses. From the coarse grains we shall produce largely pork products, and from the grasses, in the summer months, we shall produce dairy products. We have had some experience already in connection with dairy products as related to the policy which has been followed. This
Supply-Agriculture

is the policy which my hon. friend said a few moments ago brought forth considerable criticism two or three months ago, but it is not bringing forth so much criticism now. Since the beginning of the war we have followed the policy of keeping a close check on agriculture right across this country, and of not going out in advance of the time when it is necessary and calling upon everybody to produce something which we could not get rid of. We have had one experience of that kind, although we did not have to ask to have it produced; it was produced in the natural course of events. We have more wheat than we are able to get rid of for the time being, but we are fortunate in the fact that wheat is a product which will keep for a long term of years. After we hold our wheat, it will be just as good as a food product three or four years from now as it was when it was grown. That being the situation, it is fortunate that that is the product which we have in greater quantity than it can be disposed of at present, because I have no doubt that it will be used in due course to feed those people who will be requiring it.
In the meantime people must live; in the meantime people across the seas must have meat products which they cannot get elsewhere, and in the meantime we can get better returns by producing those meat products than we have been able to get for the last ten years. At the same time we shall be serving the purpose we are trying to serve in relation to the war itself. I have said that we have increased deliveries of pork products from 160,000,000 pounds in the last complete year before the war to 450,000,000 pounds this year, and we hope that the increase will be greater next year. We are fairly well assured that with the war proceeding toward a successful conclusion we shall be able to dispose of those products in a way which will be as favourable as possible under the circumstances for those who produce them.
In so far as cheese is concerned, if I remember the figures correctly, in the last year before the war we delivered about 72,000,000 pounds. Last year we delivered a little over 103,000,000 pounds, and this year we have contracted to deliver 112,000,000 pounds. Only two or three weeks ago certain newspapers in Canada were saying that we had failed entirely in our policy because we had allowed farmers to get rid of their cows, and they were not going to have the milk with which to produce cheese. I have here on my desk to-night an article written yesterday by one of the same newspapers to the effect that we have thrown away a million and a quarter dollars by putting another cent on cheese which we did not need to put on because the farmers were

going to produce the cheese anyway. I cannot understand that kind of argument, where people with one breath argue one way, and with the other breath argue another way. Nevertheless, three or four weeks ago the farmers took milk to the cheese factories in volume which produced 31 per cent less than was produced in the same week a year ago. The gradings for this last week show that in the last week for which we have a record, they took in sufficient milk to produce approximately 47 per cent more than they produced in the same week a year ago.
I quite agree with the writer of the article in this particular paper when he says that the farmers of Canada would have produced that cheese even if we had not put an extra cent on the price. I would, however, call attention to this. Britain places cheese right at the top of the list of her food necessities. She wants cheese; it has a food value, and it takes as little shipping space as any of the more important foods. It is a product which the British people are accustomed to placing in their ration of food. Our Canadian cheese is a good product. We knew, when we put an extra cent to the fifteen cents on ship at Montreal plus the one cent premium on 93 score, plus the two cents on 94 score, plus the subsidies which are provided by the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, that the farmers were getting a better price for their cheese than they had had over a long period of years extending back before the beginning of this war. We knew that they turned out within this last year more than 140,000,000 pounds of cheese, as against 100,000,000 a few years ago; that they exported to Britain
103,000,000 pounds, as against 72,000,000 pounds in the year before the war; that this year they will deliver not merely 112,000,000 pounds but probably 120,000,000 pounds or even more. Whether they do or they do not, we believe that the price which is now established will have the effect of keeping farmers delivering milk to cheese factories, as against taking it to creameries, where we have guaranteed the minimum price for the summer at a level of 30 cents in June, 30J cents in July, 31 cents in August, 31i cents in September, and 32 cents in October. With these two levels of prices established, we believe that the Canadian farmer will raise next year his production of cheese to the level it reached in the last years of the last war, and we shall be exporting, not 72,000,000 pounds as we were doing at the beginning of the war, but twice as much cheese, to Britain alone, as we sent at that time.
That is the objective we have in mind. That is our policy. We have brought the farmers through the last two years-it is

Supply-Agriculture
true, with some dissatisfaction as regards price-without encouraging the production of great surpluses which we could not get rid of for the time being, but in a condition of mind in which, as a newspaper says that was criticizing us three or four weeks ago they would have produced the product even though we had not raised the price. With the increased price level, however, they will go on next year beyond our fondest hopes in connection with the production of food.
All this is connected with the prosecution of the war. I was told the other day, by a man prominent in matters having to do with Britain's policies, that Great Britain will win this war. He did not say "if", he said that "Britain will win this war because we are going to feed the British people." When he said "we", he did not mean Canada alone; he meant all the people in the world who are associated with Britain in fighting this battle. "We are going to maintain the sea lanes. We are going to see that food gets over. As food is destroyed we are going to produce more. And," he said, "the people are going to maintain the morale which is necessary to the winning of a victory, on account of the fact that they are assured that they are going to be fed; and the battle is going to be fought through to the final conclusion."
We in Canada can play our part, and our farmers are playing their part. The government is not able, as we all agree, to pay all that the farmers ought to have, but in conjunction with Great Britain and with the United States to the south, we are trying to supply all the food we can send from this continent to Great Britain. We have done it not only by maintaining prices as high as we possibly can, and by encouraging production, but by keeping a check on the consumption of the important products, and we have tried to maintain that consumption at not a higher level than was maintained under the favourable conditions of last year.
To my hon. friend here who was talking about the circumstances of those on relief, I wish to say only this. We in Canada have passed through a very difficult period. Everyone iri this chamber knows that. He knows how we used to argue about it ten years ago; he knows that, we argued about it five years ago, and that we argued about it even two years ago.
And you are still arguing.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We have not been arguing about it very much since September, 1939. Some of us said ten years ago, five years ago, and three years ago, that the reason for the unnatural condition which existed in connection with food products, of 14873-222
which we are large producers, was that certain people were getting ready for war. There were those who scoffed at that idea, but to-day we are all convinced that they were getting ready, and they got ready to such good advantage that it is taking us from two to three years to catch up with them. We know now that preparations were being made not only in the matter of munitions, but in the matter of food. I believe every hon. member will agree with me when I say that the farmer, being a producer of food which is necessary in the same quantities per man in time of peace as in time of war, is about the only producer in Canada who was ready to supply his product in much greater quantities than could be used in this country when the war did come. He did not stop when the war broke out. He went right on producing no matter what the price was, and increased the amounts, hoping, no doubt, for some increase in prices as a result of the fact that we were at war.
He was encouraged to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: He was encouraged, and he should have been encouraged to do so.
You encouraged him.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that I encouraged him. I am afraid that if the production had not been adequate at the present time he would have said that I should have encouraged him. But I accept what he has said as a compliment. We encouraged the farmers, and the products which we asked them to produce they have available and will have available in greater quantities as the months go by. What I wish, however, to point out in this connection is, that while there may have been in Canada some few months ago about 300,000 unemployed, there was a time not very long ago when we had over 1,000,000. In other words, our unemployment rolls have been cut down considerably, and to that extent we are presumably better off than we were before.
In connection with the problem of relief, the hon. member for Mackenzie knows that it is not one which is dealt with under the Department of Agriculture. I am not trying to shirk a responsibility when I say that. Agricultural relief in western Canada was taken care of for a period of time under this department. But urban relief was never a matter which was under our charge. We did, through this department, take farm products off the market at a time when we had surpluses, and we distributed them to people who were on relief. We went even further than that. We realized that in a country such as

Supply-Agriculture

Canada people do not easily go on relief; they go on suffering a great deal of inconvenience and underfeeding in their families. Only then do they go on relief.
I think I said, on the occasion when we first took butter off the markets and gave it away, that the first thing a poor family does is to quit eating butter on account of its price and to start eating some cheap jam. Eventually they go down the list until they get to blackstrap molasses, finally giving that up, having nothing on their bread and eating it dry. That is the process they go through. We gave away butter, cheese and other products. We did not follow the stamp practice which prevails in the United States, but we did the thing that we thought was suitable to this country; and I may say what I said in reply to the question with regard to the notice that had already gone out in the province of Saskatchewan from the provincial government to the effect that there will be no relief in certain areas this year. That notice has gone out ever since we passed the peak of our unemployment condition. It is necessary from year to year to take persons off the unemployed list and off the lists of relief as conditions improve in their areas; and just as that order went out last year and relief was given later on where it was absolutely essential, so the order has gone out this year; all of which means that every person who was on the list is cut off and must make a new application again to reestablish himself as being in a position warranting the receipt of relief. I have no doubt that where it is absolutely essential it will be given.
In relation to the matter of distributing wheat or Hour, or making it possible to get it, these relief lists do make tha+ possible. I can understand, knowing conditions as I know them in the northern part of Saskatchewan, that some people have not been able to get all that they need. But knowing more particularly the frame of mind of many people in that province, I know that fathers and mothers will get along without flour for quite a while before asking for it from anyone, whether the municipal council or the government or anybody else. I know Saskatchewan well enough, however, to realize that if their neighbours know the situation, these people will not have to go without flour very long. I realize also that they should not be left in that condition and that governments should do something about the matter. But again, I have sufficient confidence in the governments of the three prairie provinces to believe that where these conditions do prevail, those governments, as soon as the facts are made known to them, will see to it that food is
fMr. Gardiner.]
got to these people. I do not wish to say anything more with regard to this particular item.

I am hopeful
that the hon. member for Fraser Valley will feel now that at least the minister has answered the question he raised with regard to eggs. In an agile manner, the minister slipped from eggs into pork, and it was quite interesting. He knows, as this committee knows, that the reason why we are able to supply more pork products to the United Kingdom, the greatest market in the world for pork products, is that Denmark is unable to ship now to the British isles. Poland, which took second place, is now unable to ship to that market, and the same is true of the Netherlands. For the last decade they have found it difficult to get their products into the United Kingdom. It was my privilege to be in Rotterdam less than a decade ago, and when I went to the steamship office and asked them to change some pounds, shillings and pence into guilders, speaking perfectly good English the man in the exchange office complained to me most bitterly, when he found that I was a Canadian, that we had stolen their market in the United Kingdom for the dairy products of the Netherlands. That was what he complained about while he was making change for me. There is the answer, and I cannot understand just why the minister should give us again one of those Napoleonic orations, slipping from eggs over to pork, picking out the choicest morsel, and discussing our exports of these commodities. I do not know why he should feel disposed to address us in the way he did- those of us who have asked questions in this house or made suggestions which we have felt to be constructive. Why should he put upon those questions or suggestions the construction he does, implying that hon. members who do this are not doing all that they can. He is wrong in that regard, Mr. Chairman. We, too, with him and with all the farmers of Canada, are trying to do a job not only on our own behalf but on behalf of our empire in seeing that they have more and more supplies. How they will get more and more supplies by our spending $35,000,000 more for the purpose of making land black on the first of July, I do not know. I know it is not to our advantage to make the lands in the west less productive. On my own farm, which has been producing fruit and vegetables, I found last Sunday that the land was entirely seeded down in mixed grain, and I found four able-bodied citizens, ordinarily resident on that farm, working in munitions plants at fifty cents an hour. That is taking up the

Supply-Agriculture
slack that is produced out west. In the long run the policy there will not make for greater supplies, not only to Great Britain but to the whole civilized world when the conflict ceases. I say to the minister: Use your $35,000,000 to pile up more and more of the gold, the gold being wheat. The minister says that wheat will keep; I say that it will keep. I must sit down now, because my hon. friend the member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) kindly gave me just three minutes. He wishes. to speak, and I shall have to stop, but I hope that when the minister rises again we shall have a reply to the observations that have been made with regard to eggs and fruit and more particularly the observations of the fruit man from Fraser Valley, the hon. member representing that constituency.

It gives me great pain to have to differ with my hon. friend who sits next to me (Mr. Harris). I differ with him in his estimation of the minister's speech, and I am afraid I am compelled to state that in my opinion he was a little off with regard to the demands of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). That hon. member did riot mention fruit; he mentioned eggs. I would explain to the committee the advantage of the trade that has been built up, started some years ago-by the present government I think-in the processing of fruit for shipment to the old country. There was a large surplus of small fruit, such as raspberries and loganberries, which would have been a dead loss but for the discovery of this method of processing it. They do it in sugar and it will keep a long time; they can ship it to the old country more or less in bulk. I hope that trade will be encouraged and supported by the government. What I was going to begin my remarks with, however, was to say that although this is late in the session and I know that language is unwelcome and words are a weariness to the house, I should like to thank the minister for his dissertation, as my hon. friend called it, or statement. I thought it was a very fine statement. Few men in this house are equal and none is superior to the minister in ability to make a statement of that kind. There was no claptrap about it, and above all, although he mentioned the war and talked about our responsibility in connection therewith and the duties that rest upon us in that connection, there was no suggestion either inferentially or directly, such as we have too often had, that if we ventured to disagree with or criticize the methods he was proposing we thereby showed ourselves disloyal or were guilty, of holding up the war effort. I am tired of these suggestions, whether implied or 14873-2224
direct. I was glad to hear the minister give his capable explanation, covering the whole ground for which his department is responsible from east to west and giving us what I thought was a clear and useful exposition.
Coming back to the hon. member for Fraser Valley, I came into the chamber last night just as he was finishing or was interrupted, being told that he was making his remarks on the wrong item and would have an opportunity to-day. It was in my mind to support him by what local knowledge I have of the matter; but when I came to look up in Hansard what he said, as reported at page 3451, I found he had made an excellent statement, so that I need do no more than say "them's my sentiments". He was dealing with eggs and the condition of poultry-keepers in his district. I, too, am familiar with the subject because I used to be in the feed business in a district where many people went in for chicken raising. They nearly all went broke, and a proportion of them, I am sorry to say, left an unpaid feed bill. When we talk about going into eggs in British Columbia, we do not mean keeping fifty or 100 hens round the back door, fed largely on table scraps, which is the best of all feed, but which we cannot obtain in quantities. Keeping hens in that way is always profitable; any one can show a profit on fifty hens; but when you try to do it on 5,000, when everything has to be bought, it is a different matter. The big egg people in British Columbia almost invariably find it a failure for that reason. You can go along road after road and see places that have been abandoned.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley spoke about the price of eggs; I presume he knew what he was talking about when he quoted figures. He said that the average price last year was 16| cents a dozen. If that was the average price, it means that the low price was very much less, and that eggs could not be produced in that province, where all the feed has to be hauled in from the prairies at a very high rate, an improperly high rate, and the eggs shipped back to the eastern market at another very high rate, at anything like that price. The hon. member for Fraser Valley said:
I should like to know whether any provision is made therein to see that the poultry producer in British Columbia, who must be guided in his prices by the export market, will be protected in exactly the same way as the .apple grower and the butter and cheese producer.
That is, will he have a guaranteed minimum price? That is what he would like to know and what I should like to know. They have done it for the munitions factories, guaranteed not only wages but a fair profit. Nearly the whole lobster catch was taken over by the
Supply-Agriculture

Minister of Fisheries, and he did well with it, almost made it pay, a remarkable thing for a government department. Wheat has been treated generously; a minimum price has been fixed for butter, the same for cheese and the same for apples. Why is it that this one industry, outstanding among all the rest, is left without any protection of that kind? We are aware that the British market is in great need of eggs. As the hon. member pointed out last night, the ten per cent or so sold in outside markets governs the domestic price. As he pointed out, we say to the Ford Motor *company and these big munition makers, "We will guarantee you not only expenses but a fair profit." Is it not fair to say to the egg producer, "We will guarantee you a fair return on the commodities you produce," which are so badly needed?
The minister spoke at some length and with great clarity as to what he or the government had been able to do in the disposal of eggs last season. He evidently did the best possible under the circumstances. But what we should like to know is, what price are we going to get for them? They have been disposed of, yes; but what is the use of raising them to sell at a price below the cost of production? As I said, you can keep two or three score hens and make them profitable; but when you get into the larger numbers, you have to have the money coming in to pay for the feed, which has to be brought in from the prairies at a rate about half as much again as it should be and half as much again as is charged for export to China or the British empire. The export rate is much lower than the domestic rate. It does not seem fair or just that when the railway hauls a carload of No. 1 wheat from Calgary to Vancouver for export at a certain rate, I think it is twenty cents a hundred pounds, yet it is entitled to charge forty cents, now cut in some instances to thirty cents, for identically the same wheat for the use of British Columbia industry. It does not make sense.
I should like to have an answer to the question. Why is it impossible to peg the price of eggs? Is it lack of money? No; we are dealing in millions; it cannot be that. Is it lack of interest? No; it cannot be that; the minister has taken an interest in the disposal of eggs. Is it lack of unity among the farmers? Is it the age-old antipathy of farmers to cooperation? If they were to form a union, perhaps they would be listened to, but we are foolish enough to divide our influence between Liberals, Tories, C.C.F.'s and so forth. If the egg producers would get together and demand their rights, they would probably be listened to with greater attention.

We want, do we not, to preserve this industry to produce this greatly needed food for Britain; we want to keep up an industry by which numbers of our people can live; but if something is not done, they will be put out of business. It seems to me an unanswerable proposition. The government have taken care of all these other people, the lobster fishers, the producers of cheese, butter, apples, all except the egg producers who are left to sink or swim, and I am afraid they are going to sink.
Let us give to the government the credit that is coming to them. A few months ago they did use their influence to get the railways to put in a considerabe reduction in the rate on No. 3 wheat and better. We were running short of the lower grades and were not allowed to ship the higher grades under the lower rate. The government did help us there, and for the moment we are allowed to put in higher grade wheat at this medium rate which, however, is still much too high. But that is not sufficient. They made an offer to the eastern provinces to pay half the freight rate on the lower grades if the province would pay the other half, but the British Columbia government did not have the gumption to follow that up. Instead, they got this temporary and rather illusive advantage of having Nos. 1, 2 and 3 grade wheat included in the lower rate. There is plenty of No. 4 wheat still on the prairies, and therefore this rate really does not do us much good. Is the minister going to help us? I do not speak for myself because I do not own a hen, I would not if I had the opportunity; I speak on behalf of the people who are trying to make a living raising chickens, in the constituency of the hon. member for Fraser Valley, New Westminster and some other ridings on the lower mainland and also parts of Vancouver island. I would just say this. If the minister does not do something for the British Columbia poultryman, he is going to have to go out of business.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Just in case I forget this later on, I should say that in addition to securing a reduced rate on feed, the government took up with the railways the question of getting a reduced rate on export eggs, and some reduction has been made. I am not able to give the reduction at the moment, but I just wish to make that statement now.
Under the arrangements now being made, the price paid for eggs varies from about sixteen cents to twenty cents a dozen. I quite agree that this is not a sufficiently high price to satisfy those who are producing eggs, but that is the price being paid under the arrangements I mentioned earlier this evening.

Supply-Agriculture
What was the price?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
From sixteen to twenty cents, depending upon the part of Canada in which the producer lives. As to why eggs have not been dealt with as some other products have, I would remind hon. members that only a very small percentage of our eggs, either before the war began or since, have gone to Britain. I should think that percentage would not be more than one per cent before the war, and perhaps a little more than that since. On the other hand, we have sent 70 per cent of our cheese to Britain and 64 per cent of our pork products; about 70 per cent of our wheat has been going for export, although not all to Britain, and about 50 per cent of our apples went to Britain before the war.
In the beginning we tried to deal with those products which had been most affected by the war; and, as I stated on a previous occasion, we tried to deal with the products the market for which had been destroyed by the war. The first two products were tobacco and apples. We did nothing with regard to tobacco, except to induce Britain to take some of it. We did something with regard to apples and other similar products. Then we tried to increase the return to the growers. One hon. member said to-night that I had dealt with the wheat problem in a fine way, from the point of view of the wheat growers. The wheat growers do not have that opinion. They believe, as a matter of fact, that since 1938 we have lowered the price of wheat, and that is so. In 1938 the' price of wheat was eighty cents; it is now pegged at seventy cents. In 1937 the pegged price was 87J cents. We have not pegged the price of wheat at that height since the beginning of the war, and since 1938 we have been asking the wheat grower to put up with conditions more difficult than those which existed before the beginning of the war.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Largely because of the great surplus of wheat I mentioned in the beginning, which makes it impossible for the government to do otherwise at the moment, not because that is our desire but on account of the great surpluses which have been piling up.
To come back to the question of eggs, there is still only a very small proportion of our egg production going to Britain. We have not been letting this matter go without giving any thought to it, but I really believe eggs are in a different class from that of some of the other products. Particularly is
that so for this reason, that probably we should find some way of basing the price of eggs in Canada upon the consumption of eggs in Canada rather than upon the consumption of eggs in Britain. It appears to me that the price of our eggs up to the present time has been pretty well fixed by what we could get for the small surplus that we have been sending out of this country.
I am sure the hon. member for Comox-Alberni will agree that it would not be the easiest possible thing to fix egg prices in this dominion, where distances are so great and conditions vary so much. In British Columbia they feed and house their chickens as they should be fed and housed. On the prairies we let them run wild and feed them not only on what is left from the table but very often on grasshoppers, which do not make the flavour of the eggs very enticing. People are not inclined to eat a second "grasshopper" egg if they can avoid doing so. In Ontario there is not the same care taken in the feeding and housing of chickens as in British Columbia. I travel in Ontario quite often, and I find that most of the chicken flocks in this province still have the run of the farms, and one cannot produce good eggs with the hens running all around, picking up anything they can find to eat. In the maritimes there is probably a little more care taken in connection with poultry. Therefore it is not the easiest thing to regulate the price of eggs in a country like Canada. We might be able to handle the situation as it exists in British Columbia and in the extreme east; but the man in the middle west, who just lets his hens run wild and regards whatever he gets for the eggs as something extra, presents a greater problem, and it is difficult to control the prices of eggs under these conditions. We have, however, given the matter considerable thought, and we hope to arrive at some conclusion which will be of greater help than anything we have been able to do up to the present.

I am somewhat at a disadvantage in taking part in this discussion because I have been attending a meeting of the war expenditures committee. I am glad some concession has been given the poultry raisers of British Columbia with regard to the freight on feed grain, but I should like to ask the minister why nothing has been done along the same line for the people of the maritime provinces. The government and agricultural societies of Nova Scotia have been appealing to the federal government for a considerable time for some concession which would enable the surplus feed grains of the
351S
Supply-Agriculture

prairie provinces to be delivered to the stock feeders and poultry raisers of the maritime provinces. Up to the present time, as I understand it, the department has been unable to grant this concession, but we are still hoping that something may be done.

I wish to protest against the importation of small new potatoes from the United States. Hundreds of cars of Alabama and California new potatoes came in during May when our potato growers were selling their potatoes at less than half the cost of production. These United States potatoes are of a grade and size which our growers are not allowed to market in Canada.
Supply-Agriculture

Foreign exchange is being used to bring in these potatoes. An order in council was put through on March 25 which was supposed to cure this condition, but it did not. They changed the grade from U.S. grade 1, size B, to U.S. grade 1, size A, but a proviso was included that until August 31 inclusive in each calendar year a minimum diameter of If inches was the only size requirement for new potatoes. The United States have new potatoes all the year round, and therefore small potatoes can be shipped in here any month of the year.

I am sorry the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has left the chamber. When he was talking about vitamins or the sources of vitamins, I should have liked to suggest to him that he would better have considered the fish on our eastern coast. Ten times the amount of the proper vitamins can be obtained from ten cents worth of cod-liver oil as can be obtained from ten cents worth of fruit juices.

I have not received an answer from the minister to my question as to why the maritime provinces have not been given the same concessions as have been granted to the poultry raisers of British Columbia in connection with freight rates on grain for poultry feeding.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
In all the discussion I forgot the hon. member's question. Last winter the eastern provinces, particularly the maritimes, asked us to give some assistance in the bringing of feed grains from Fort William. A little later on, the provinces of Quebec and Ontario became involved in the discussion. In the first instance we did agree to pay half the freight on feed grain from Montreal to the maritime provinces, but that was not considered satisfactory. The other two provinces were brought into the discussion, and we finally offered to pay the freight on feed grain from Fort William to all the five eastern provinces. After we had made that offer, much to our surprise the only province that took it up was Ontario, which perhaps needed it the least. They took 3,200,000 bushels and an additional sixty carloads. Before they could stop buying, they had another sixty carloads, and since no one else had come in we extended the offer to those sixty carloads. The other provinces came to the conclusion that it would be better policy for them not to take advantage of the offer. Probably, if we had agreed to pay all the freight, or if we had agreed to enter into an arrangement by which they could charge half the freight to the farmer, they would have accepted. We took the position that the intention was to give the farmer cheaper feed and to make feed available to him on the same basis as 
it was available in the other provinces. We thought that anything which was allowed should be paid by the governments and that the farmers should get the full benefit of the price, less the freight. It was left in that way, but the other provinces did not take advantage of it.

What about
the concessions on grain for poultry purposes to British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That rate aplies only
to British Columbia. Freight rates generally are dealt with by the transport board, and I understand that the position always taken by that board, as it was taken by the old board of railway commissioners, is that they will not set up any rates for any particular section of Canada which discriminate against any other section. When rates were established as between the prairies and British Columbia, the fact as to whether there was discrimination was taken into consideration. In connection with the shipment of grain from the prairies to the maritimes we went first to the transport board, and they took the position that they could not give a special rate for the maritimes without discriminating against the provinces in between. They finally took the position that they would not give a special rate even when all five provinces were being considered, because there would be some discrimination. After that decision had been given, we agreed to pay half the freight. We said to the provinces that we were quite prepared to pay half the freight provided they could get the railways to take part of the other half and then they take what was left. They again went to the railways, and the same position was taken, that there would be discrimination and, therefore, they would not reduce the rates.

A short time before I left old
Ireland to come to Canada, one of my neighbours who was a farmer thought he would wean his dog off eating, and he succeeded in doing that, but the dog died a few days afterwards. I think all will admit that that is a mean trick for anyone to try. Having listened, however, to the hon. member for Danforth, and also to statements of the policies of ministers of agriculture for the last number of years, not alone in the Liberal government, but in the Conservative government as well, I feel that they have been trying to wean the dog off eating, because the policy pursued by both those parties has been to starve out the farmer. I do not know whether in their opinion it is sound or sane business, but to my mind it is insane business. No country can survive unless its farmers are prosperous;

Supply-Agriculture
and I might suggest that they should do what has been practised by a number of other industries in Canada for years past. If farmers were organized as they should be, they would be able to demand and obtain their costs of production plus a reasonable profit. If they did not get that cost and profit, they would do what the industrialists did in August, 1939, shortly before the war started; they would go to the government and demand certain things, and they would have their demands granted, as the industrialists did when they had their profit restrictions removed by orders in council which were imposed by parliament only that spring.
I am not going to suggest for a moment that the farmers go on strike at this time, but I would assert that, if they did so, they would be doing only what other interests in Canada have done in years past, and, perhaps, would do yet if their requests were not met.
The Minister of Agriculture has admitted on several occasions that we as farmers are entitled to better prices for our products, and says that the reason why we are not getting better prices for those products is that there is a surplus. If industry had a surplus of aeroplanes, Bren guns, ships or anything else, I wonder whether they would give them away at half the cost of production. They would not; they are too well organized and have too much control over governments to-day to do anything of that kind. But because farmers are unorganized, and, many of them, underfed, they are easy to control. For the past number of years, as far back as I can remember-thirty years at least-we have been controlled because we are underfed and are not able, owing to conditions which have been imposed on us and which we are not organized to fight, to demand the rights which properly belong to us.
Time after time in this house I have heard the Prime Minister and other hon. members plead for Canadian unity. They have declared that we must have equality of sacrifice. I ask the Minister of Agriculture and other ministers who are on the front benches tonight, is there an equality of sacrifice, and are all the industries in Canada treated alike? Inevitably the answer must be, no, the farming industry is being sabotaged and sooner or later must go down.
Since I came to the house we have presented arguments supported by figures issued under the authority of the government, to establish the truth of what I have said. I have no doubt that the government has sufficient evidence from every comer of this chamber to prove that we are not getting a square deal. The other day I quoted figures of wheat prices ',4873-223
between 1926 and 1929. Upon the basis of that period, labour and industry alike are living under conditions equal to those which prevailed at that time. I quoted figures to show that if the farmers were paid on the basis of the average obtained for wheat at that time, we would be getting $1.35 a bushel. Instead of that, we receive 70 cents basis No. 1 northern at Fort William.
Advantage is also taken of the farmer in the matter of grades. I know of instances where wheat which graded No. 1 northern when threshing commenced was later brought down to No. 3. Nothing was done about the matter; the farmer had to take the rap. Such conditions should be remedied. Perhaps part of the poor success of our recruiting is due to some of the deals which have been handed out to the farmer.
To keep people underfed is to keep them under control. Something will have to be done. We must have forward-thinking people at the head of the government, men of progressive minds who will figure things out from the long-range point of view. The government travels just as fast' as it is pushed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

The hon. member is in order when speaking on that subject, but not in reviewing statements which, to use his own words, he has already made.
I am discussing conditions in connection with marketing.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Might I further call
attention to the fact that the marketing of wheat is not under the Department of Agriculture at all; it is under the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the proper place to discuss it is on the estimates of that department.
Mr. Chairman, that is just a side-line. We shall have a chance to discuss it later on. But-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is out of order.
I say that the marketing of wheat has been discussed by other hon. members, and not a word was said against it. That is not fair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I thought it was Fair.

Yes; Fair is speaking, but he is not getting fair treatment, because on

Supply-Agriculture

different occasions I have been ruled out of order when I tried to answer questions raised by other speakers. I do not think that is fair.
Are you Fair?
Yes, I am Fair. I am not to be kidded, anjuvay.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This should bring to the attention of hon. members the difficulties into which the chairman falls when he gives latitude and the rule is not strictly adhered to. It appears that when I was away from the committee the discussion was broadened, and when I came back I noticed that hon. members were not talking to the item. But we must draw the line somewhere.
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate your position, and I know that hon. members, including myself, have got out of bounds, but it is not fair that I should be singled out rather than anyone else.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is the last one to whom I would not be fair.

I should have the same rights as other members.
I have here a statement of the United States programme in connection with the production of foodstuffs. Perhaps I had better read this. This is production, not marketing, but I come to the marketing part in the same article:
Under the expanded programme, and . . . assuming continuation of existing price relationships and taking seasonal price variations into account, the department will make purchases in the open market to support long term prices (Chicago basis) at levels approximately as follows: Hogs, cwt., $9; dairy products (basis of butter, lb.), 31 cents; chickens, lb., 15 cents; eggs, doz., 22 cents. It was pointed out that these prices would be subjected to the customary commercial differentials for market grades and qualities.
As regards eggs, somebody has raised the question, and it may be in order to make one brief protest. I understand that the grades are not what they should be. The price per dozen is raised, but the grades are being changed sufficiently to keep the price down. Possibly more will be heard on that point when the question of egg production comes up on a later item.
I do not know that there is much use in saying any more. The government has got a programme, and apparently it is going to follow it out, with the result that it will sabotage to a considerable degree, as it has done in the past, the industry of agriculture.

I did not intend to speak on this item. I have been waiting to discuss another subject, but I thought I would point out that this whole discussion has been out

of order for an hour and a half, although I have been ruled out of order on two or three occasions recently. Even to-day, when I undertook to discuss a certain question on a bill, the minister suggested that it would be better for me to leave the matter until we came to item 29. Yesterday I was ruled out of order on the question of production. This discussion on marketing has been out of order to-night. Last night one or two hon. members switched to a discussion which they thought they could carry on, but they were ruled out. The minister has been the chief transgressor. He gave a careful and interesting outline of the situation with regard to markets in Britain, and he covered everything. He covered item 26 and item 24; he spoke about the bonusing bill; he referred to summerfallowing; he discussed the advertisements discouraging the growing of more wheat; he mentioned butter, cattle, cheese, hogs and feed grain-and all this under the question of production. He might have told us what will be done with feed grains this year, because the Minister of Trade and Commerce has tabled an order in council which practically makes it impossible for the farmer to do anything this year except under the most drastic conditions. The minister covered a great range of subjects.
He did it satisfactorily.

Yes; I do not deny that he did. No one is better able to do it than the minister. He said that the one industry which was in a position when the war broke out to produce the materials necessary to assist in large measure in winning the war was agriculture. I suggest that it would be well if he would do something to make it possible for the farmer to receive for his products a price bearing some favourable comparison with prices paid for other commodities. I am not going to take up more time now. I agree with what the hon. member for Danforth said. The condition in Great Britain with regard to bacon and dairy products is attributable largely to the war, although the minister has boasted about increasing our exports of these products to that market. Of course, it is a splendid thing that we are able to supply these products, and the farmer will do his part to produce the necessary commodities from time to time and to continue producing, even at a loss, for the purpose of winning the war. I rose at this stage merely to lodge a protest, because, as I say, I have been ruled out of order several times in the last week, and to-night this whole discussion, for at least an hour and a half, has been altogether out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: All hon. members will recall that some weeks ago we gave an undertaking to certain hon. gentlemen that in view of the fact that we wanted to wind up the discussion on the wheat acreage reduction, we would permit, under this item, the discussion of the question which the hon. member for Lambton-Kent raised to-night. The discussion was out of order, but that undertaking was given. That is one reason for the discussion that took place to-night.
Do I understand that any one of us who wished to ask questions about wheat acreage reduction should have done so on this item?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No. I would suggest 'that there is an opportunity for discussing the administration of it under the estimate having to do with prairie farm assistance. However, we said that we would give an opportunity to those particular members to discuss the question on one of the administration items in agriculture, and the only administration item was this one under marketing.
I myself was waiting to speak on item 30.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The discussion on corn was carried on for the same reason.

When the committee rose last night we were discussing apples, and I wanted to say a few words on the situation in that regard. I congratulate the minister and the department upon what they have done for the apple growers of Canada. The attitude they have taken towards marketing and control of apples in the dominion has been a wonderful thing for the producers. Without that assistance it would have been difficult if not impossible to market our apples owing to the loss of the export market. The government have spent many thousands of dollars in advertising. In fact, not only governments but cooperative fruit growers associations have done so. I hold in my hand one advertisement in the form of the picture of an apple. It is a good apple too. We are told to eat more apples, that apples are good for the health, and so forth. During the past few weeks I have visited some of the camps throughout the country, and I must say that the apples used there are a long way from the sort of apple depicted in this advertisement. I understand that these apples are domestic grade. There is a great difference in domestic grades, and if we are simply to accept anything as domestic grade, we are going to get down to rather poor apples. When two and a quarter inch apples are allowed to go into 14873-2231
domestic grades, and the apple has spots or fungus the size of a five cent piece, although it complies with the law as a domestic apple, we are a long way from the sort of thing we are advertising. My contention is that if we advertise apples in this way we should try to give the people a product that more closely resembles the thing we advertise. In our county there is a difference in the grading of domestics.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry, but I cannot see the relationship between the item under discussion and the question of grading apples, unless there is something which has escaped me. I am afraid that the discussion is out of order.
I understood that we could discuss these matters on item 20.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are on item 22. and apples would come under fruit and vegetables.

I suggest that it might be just as well to dispose of the question now. What I was saying was that if we are going to advertise our apples in this way we should give the people what we are advertising or something near it. In our' county a great many growers sell their apples as domestic. There might be forty or fifty per cent No. 1 in them, and the people who buy a hamper or a barrel of those domestic apples get a good grade. But when we grade them as the law says down to a fair domestic and take all the good ones out, which they are doing and selling them to these camps, I think we are getting down where we shall not be advertising our apples in the right way. There seems to be a lack of inspection on the part of someone in allowing this grade of apples to be sold. I saw in some of those camps apples that were not No. 3s by any means. I had one inspector go and look at some-

Order. Unless the
committee is willing to take items 26 and 22 together, I shall be in trouble with my own ruling if I allow the discussion to go on along these lines. Is it the pleasure of the committee to take at the same time items 22 and 26?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I was speaking about the grading of apples. If we are going to sell our apples we should sell them in accordance with our advertising. I was at some of those camps and saiw apples that were not No. 3, and the inspection must have been very poor to allow those apples to be sold. We are

paying inspectors; we have quite an inspection service; we have a fruit branch that is supposed to look after these matters. But as an apple grower I do not think we are doing justice to the business in allowing this kind of apples to be sold. I pass this information on to the minister, for I know I would not be allowed to send them out of my orchard. I understand that these apples are put in oold storage, bought from some cooperative concern, and I cannot understand why they were allowed to go into that cold storage plant, or allowed to get into the camp. We have inspectors; they are well paid; if we have not enough, let us get more, and control this thing.
I also want to congratulate the department upon what they have done for the apple grower.
The minister mentioned dehydrated apples. What is the surplus of dehydrated apples now?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have not the exact figures as to what we have left, but the amount is getting very low. We have no great quantity left.

I do not believe there is one woman in twenty-five throughout Canada who really knows what can be done with dehydrated apples. Some different advertising should be done in regard to the matter, because dehydrated apples will make much better apple pie or apple sauce than fresh apples.
I do not agree.

The apples which the hon. member mentioned are put in storage for some months and then they have not the flavour. I agree, however, with the hon. member with regard to the grading of apples. In Peterborough county I do not think one can get a decent apple at less than sixty cents a peck after October 1, and they are not properly graded at that. That is why people are starting to use dehydrated apples.

In the details given on page 68 of the estimates under "marketing service", I see two home economists and one assistant demonstrator and lecturer. What are the duties of these persons, and how do they contribute to the marketing service?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Their work is to provide recipes and so forth, to overcome the very difficulty mentioned by the hon. member for Peterborough West, namely, to teach women how to use dehydrated apples. We could use half a dozen more of them to good advantage but did not think it wise to spend the money at the present time.

That raises a question which I think is of vital importance. We are dealing now with one of the primary industries and primary products of Canada. If secondary industry finds it expedient and advisable to have a merchandising service and actually goes out and demonstrates the value and usefulness of its products, then it seems to me that this department might very well adopt those methods which have been found efficient in the promotion of the use of the natural products of Canada in their natural state. We are all familiar with the methods adopted even by manufacturers of chewing gum in demonstrating the uses of the article. Nearly every successful manufacturing industry in Canada has found it profitable and expedient to increase the consumption of the product or service which it is purveying by actually getting out and selling or merchandising that product or service. We had one example two years ago of what this department can accomplish in "selling" to the Canadian people, our own home people, the value of the Canadian apple in its raw state. We are all familiar with the satisfactory and gratifying result of that in increasing the use of our apple crop.
What disturbs me-I referred to it once before-is that there seems to be a tendency to do the very opposite of what successful industry and commerce do when faced with a similar situation; that is, instead of expanding our appropriation for advertising and demonstrating the value and usefulness of the commodity, the department is spending less money. The minister has said that we could profitably use half a dozen more demonstrators. If, by the employment of six or eight or ten or twenty home economists-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman speaking to item 28 now?
No; I am speaking to item 22.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is no decrease in that item.

The minister has just
stated that the department could use six or eight more home economists and demonstrators in connection with the marketing services, and it is my suggestion that instead of contracting our expenditures in connection with the merchandising and marketing of agricultural products in Canada, we could and should increase our appropriation for that purpose.

I was surprised a few
moments ago to hear the hon. member for

Supply-Agriculture
Qu'Appelle state that during the last couple of days he had been called to order on more than one occasion. I can scarcely credit that statement, for in the course of his remarks during the last few days I have heard him express greater approval of the policies of the government, and a greater degree of confidence in the Minister of Agriculture, than in the last five years. So eulogistic were those references that I quite anticipate that during the summer months the hon. member for Qu'Appelle will be going through the constituencies of Saskatchewan expressing sentiments similar to those which were expressed to me by a former confrere of the hon. gentleman, the late member for Parkdale, whom we all respected and admired, who told me that he thought the present minister was the best Minister of Agriculture Canada ever had.
To what item is the hon. member referring?

I am marketing the
Minister of Agriculture. Under this item of marketing I should like to bring one matter to the attention of the minister. In British Columbia, under the provincial marketing act which has been declared intra vires by the courts, they have set up either one or two companies which control the fruit industry of that province. There is a monopoly, which is subsidized by the dominion government, particularly in connection with apples, to the extent of 81,750,000. That monopoly is further protected by the difference in freight rates; by the usual rates of duty that obtain; by the dumping duties that apply during certain seasons of the year, concerning which we are receiving notices every other day; by the 10 per cent general duty, put into effect last fall, and finally by the 10 per cent foreign exchange rate. Therefore the fruit industry of British Columbia is to-day the most highly protected industry anywhere in this country, and by reason of that protection they have set up a monopoly with regard to the sale of fruit on the prairies.
I am not going to detract from the quality of the fruit produced in British Columbia, but they are exercising the monopoly they enjoy in this way. Dealers on the prairies [DOT] who have been in business for years are denied the right to purchase fruit from this monopoly. They have the cash; they are willing to live up to every condition imposed by the monopoly; yet they cannot buy the fruit. The monopoly takes to itself the right to select its own dealers and designate the terms upon which its products shall be sold. I protest most emphatically against any monopoly, subsidized and protected as this one is, selecting
its dealers here and there and driving out of business other individuals who have been in the business for a period of years.
We have a great many monopolies in this country, and it seems to me that we who live on the prairies are the victims of all of them. We have the fruit and lumber monopolies of the Pacific coast. We have the industrial monopoly of eastern Canada. We in Saskatchewan, in the centre of Canada, a million people, sit there battered and bruised, pillaged and plundered, raped and robbed, sucked and squeezed, the ready victims of the voracious. I wish to raise an emphatic protest against the continued operation of this monopoly, and to ask the minister to exercise his usual ability in coping with this situation. I ask that he require this monopoly at least to extend its privileges to all those who have been in this line of business for many years.

The hon. member has
just delivered a carefully phrased and rather severe stricture on the fruit industry of British Columbia, which I do not think it would be possible to answer completely in ten minutes. It does occur to me, however, that if conditions are one-tenth as bad as he has described them, he has a ready opportunity at hand to gain redress, about which as a lawyer he must know a good deal. He can make use of the machinery under the Combines Investigation Act to lay bare the wickedness of this combine.
That has been attempted already, but they have no jurisdiction because this is a provincial company, authorized and approved under provincial legislation.

I suggest that a provincial statute cannot give that company rights within the province of Saskatchewan, because that is outside the jurisdiction of that act. I therefore repeat that if the situation is as bad as he has described it-and I am not ready to subscribe to all the points he made in his rapidly painted picture-he has at his disposal an opportunity to make use of the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. I do not accept his statement that this has been tried and is not efficacious for the reason he gave.

The question raised
by the hon. member for Fraser Valley with regard to the price of eggs either was not answered satisfactorily by the minister, or I failed to hear it.

I am interested in this matter of the price of eggs. It seems to me that the minister should be in a position to give us some specific statement regarding Canada's proposals in respect of eggs.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: If we are to keep to the item, then the hon. member is really discussing item No. 27.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When a question has been raised and the minister has answered, if any hon. member is not satisfied with his answer, then the hon. member's remedy lies in voting against the item. But it is against the rules of the committee to repeat an argument or to repeat a question. The question has been developed respecting remedies to be applied in connection with the price of eggs. The minister has given a lengthy answer as to the reasons why the price of eggs has not been regulated to a greater extent by the department. I repeat the same questions over and over again is against the rules of the committee.

I am not entirely sure that I know what this is all about. I have been trying to learn ever since I came into the chamber to-night. It would seem that we are discussing a question of marketing; surely the price of eggs is connected with marketing?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, but it has been discussed already. The very same question was put to the minister, and he answered it. There is a rule against repetition of the same question. That is the point I am drawing to the attention of hon. members.
Surely that does not prevent me from commenting upon what the minister has said?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is quite permissible for the hon. member to comment upon the minister's answer, but he must not repeat the question to which an answer has already been given. That would entail tedious repetition, and it is clearly prohibited by the rules.

It seems to me
strange that Canada cannot give any sort of commitment as to what the price of eggs will be. I am not asking the question. It was pointed out, however, that the United States is offering to buy eggs at twenty-two cents a dozen, and that the price will remain at that figure until June 30, 1943. My general comment is that the price of eggs throughout Canada is very uncertain. No man can have any assurance whatsoever, if he buys a number of baby chicks this spring, develops them and goes into the production of eggs, as to what the price will be.

If we want to have egg production in Canada, then, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, the one way to get egg production is to guarantee the price at which producers of eggs will be able to carry on. No such price has been guaranteed, and it is my contention that the minister and the Department of Agriculture should be prepared to make that guarantee. If the United States can guarantee a price of twenty-two cents a dozen, then we should be able to come somewhere near that. The objection I had was that the minister had not given us any clear or definite statement.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: If I might again draw attention to the fact, I would point out that this discussion should be under item 27. I have already answered the question twice, and I would be out of order in answering it again. Everything connected with the sale of eggs com es under the item for live stock and live stock products. I should like to have one or two of these items passed to-night, even if it is almost eleven o'clock. We have been discussing about eight items at one time.
I grant that all that may be true. I have been sitting quietly, listening to other hon. members talk, and I had gathered that the matters to which I have referred were under discussion.

speechtext: When we reach item 27 I shall be prepared to answer the hon. member.

That is just fine. I am concerned about learning what we are discussing. All I wish to say can be said under item 27, and if I am permitted to do so I shall be satisfied. I do not wish to be out of order.
